Java OOPs Concepts - 200 Interview Questions and Answers | Page 2

Section 1: OOP Fundamentals, Classes and Objects

Q1. What is Object-Oriented Programming (OOP)?

Ans: OOP is a programming paradigm that models software as a collection of objects that combine

data (fields) and behavior (methods). It focuses on reusability, modularity and maintainability using

four pillars: encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism and abstraction.

Q2. What are the four main pillars of OOP?

Ans: Encapsulation (bundling data with methods and hiding internals), Inheritance (acquiring

properties of a parent class), Polymorphism (one interface, many forms) and Abstraction (exposing

only essential details).

Q3. What is a class in Java?

Ans: A class is a blueprint or template that defines the state (fields) and behavior (methods) common

to all objects of that type. It does not consume memory for instance data until an object is created.

Q4. What is an object in Java?

Ans: An object is a runtime instance of a class. It has state (values of its fields), behavior (methods)

and identity (a unique reference in the heap).

Q5. How do you create an object in Java?

Ans: Using the new keyword, e.g. Car c = new Car();. Other ways include reflection

(Class.newInstance / Constructor.newInstance), cloning, deserialization and factory

methods.

Q6. What is the difference between a class and an object?

Ans: A class is a logical blueprint defined once at compile time; an object is a physical instance of

that blueprint created at runtime. Many objects can be created from one class, each with its own

state.

Q7. Where are objects and references stored in memory?

Ans: Objects live on the heap. Local reference variables live on the stack (inside stack frames) and

point to the heap objects. Static members are stored in the Metaspace (method area) associated with

the class.

Q8. What is a reference variable?

Ans: A variable that holds the address (reference) of an object rather than the object itself. Multiple

reference variables can point to the same object.

Q9. What is a constructor?

Ans: A special method used to initialize a new object. It has the same name as the class, has no

return type, and is invoked automatically when an object is created with new.

Q10. What are the types of constructors in Java?

Ans: Default (no-arg) constructor, user-defined no-arg constructor, and parameterized constructor.

Java also has copy-constructor style patterns, though not a built-in type.

Q11. What is a default constructor?

Ans: A no-argument constructor supplied by the compiler only when the class declares no

constructor at all. It calls super() implicitly and initializes fields to default values.

Q12. Does the compiler provide a default constructor if you define a parameterized one?

Ans: No. Once any constructor is declared, the compiler does not generate the default constructor. If

you need a no-arg constructor you must write it explicitly.

↑ Topic index
Book page 6

Java OOPs Concepts - 200 Interview Questions and Answers | Page 3

Q13. What is constructor overloading?

Ans: Defining multiple constructors in the same class with different parameter lists (number, type or

order). The compiler chooses the matching one at object creation.

Q14. Can a constructor be private?

Ans: Yes. Private constructors are used in Singleton classes, utility classes, factory-method patterns

and to prevent instantiation or subclassing.

Q15. Can a constructor be final, static or abstract?

Ans: No. Constructors cannot be inherited or overridden, so final is meaningless; they are tied to

instance creation, so static and abstract are not allowed.

Q16. Can a constructor return a value?

Ans: No. A constructor has no return type, not even void. If you add a return type, it becomes an

ordinary method, not a constructor.

Q17. What is constructor chaining?

Ans: Calling one constructor from another. this(...) calls another constructor of the same class;

super(...) calls a parent-class constructor. Chaining avoids duplicate initialization code.

Q18. What are the rules for this() and super() calls in a constructor?

Ans: Each must be the first statement in the constructor, so you cannot use both in the same

constructor. If neither is written, the compiler inserts super() automatically.

Q19. What is the this keyword?

Ans: A reference to the current object. It is used to disambiguate fields from parameters, call other

constructors or methods, and pass the current object as an argument.

Q20. Can this be used in a static context?

Ans: No. Static methods and blocks belong to the class, not to any instance, so there is no current

object and this is not available.

Q21. What is the static keyword?

Ans: It marks a member as belonging to the class rather than to instances. Static variables are

shared by all objects, static methods can be called without creating an object, and static blocks run

once at class loading.

Q22. What is a static variable?

Ans: A class-level variable with a single copy shared across all instances. It is initialized when the

class is loaded.

Q23. What is the difference between instance and static variables?

Ans: Instance variables are per-object and stored on the heap with the object; static variables are

per-class and shared by all objects. Instance variables need an object to be accessed, static ones

can be accessed by the class name.

Q24. What is a static method and what are its restrictions?

Ans: A method that belongs to the class. It can access only static members directly, cannot use this

or super, and cannot be overridden (it can only be hidden).

Q25. Why is the main method static?

Ans: So the JVM can invoke it without creating an object of the class. The signature is public

static void main(String[HTML edition with clickable topic index and page navigation args).

Java OOPs Concepts - 200 Interview Questions and Answers | Page 4

Q26. What is a static block?

Ans: A block static { ... } executed once when the class is first loaded, before the main

method and before any object is created. It is used for complex static initialization.

Q27. What is an instance initializer block?

Ans: A block { ... } without a keyword that runs every time an object is created, after the super

constructor call and before the rest of the constructor body.

Q28. In what order do static blocks, instance blocks and constructors execute?

Ans: Static blocks (once, at class load) first, then for each object: instance initializer blocks and field

initializers in textual order, then the constructor body. Parent class parts run before child class parts.

Q29. What is the final keyword?

Ans: It restricts modification: a final variable cannot be reassigned, a final method cannot be

overridden, and a final class cannot be extended.

Q30. What is the difference between final, finally and finalize?

Ans: final is a modifier; finally is a block in try-catch that always executes; finalize() is an

Object method called by the garbage collector before reclaiming an object (deprecated since Java 9).

Q31. What is a blank final variable?

Ans: A final variable declared without an initial value. It must be initialized exactly once, either in the

constructor or in an initializer block.

Q32. Can we change the state of an object referred to by a final reference?

Ans: Yes. final makes the reference non-reassignable, not the object immutable. You can still

modify the object's fields through that reference.

Q33. What are the different types of variables in Java?

Ans: Local variables (inside methods, on the stack), instance variables (non-static fields in the object)

and static/class variables (shared per class).

Q34. What are the default values of instance variables?

Ans: 0 for numeric types, false for boolean, '' for char and null for references. Local

variables have no default and must be initialized before use.

Q35. What is a package in Java?

Ans: A namespace that groups related classes and interfaces. It prevents name conflicts, controls

access and helps organize code. It is declared using the package statement.

Q36. What is the difference between import and package?

Ans: package declares where the current class belongs; import lets you refer to classes from other

packages by their simple name.

Q37. What is a static import?

Ans: import static allows direct use of static members of a class without qualifying them with the

class name, e.g. import static java.lang.Math.PI;.

Q38. What is method overloading?

Ans: Defining multiple methods with the same name in the same class but different parameter lists. It

is resolved at compile time and is a form of compile-time polymorphism.

Q39. Can we overload a method by changing only the return type?

Ans: No. The return type is not part of the method signature for overloading, so the compiler reports a

duplicate method error.

↑ Topic index
Book page 8

Java OOPs Concepts - 200 Interview Questions and Answers | Page 5

Q40. Can we overload the main method?

Ans: Yes, but the JVM only calls public static void main(String[Combined in ascending filename order args) as the entry

point. Other overloads must be called explicitly.

Q41. What is a method signature?

Ans: The method name plus its parameter types in order. Return type, access modifier and

exceptions are not part of it.

Q42. How does Java resolve overloaded methods when exact types do not match?

Ans: In order: exact match, widening primitive conversion, autoboxing/unboxing, then varargs. If

ambiguity remains, a compile-time error occurs.

Q43. What are varargs?

Ans: A feature that lets a method accept zero or more arguments of the same type using Type...

name. It is treated as an array inside the method and must be the last parameter.

Q44. Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?

Ans: Java is always pass-by-value. For objects, the value of the reference is copied, so the method

can modify the object's state but cannot make the caller's reference point elsewhere.

Q45. What is garbage collection?

Ans: The automatic process in which the JVM reclaims memory of objects that are no longer

reachable from any live reference. Developers cannot force it; System.gc() is only a hint.

Q46. When does an object become eligible for garbage collection?

Ans: When no live thread can reach it through any chain of references, for example after its reference

is set to null, goes out of scope, or an island of isolated objects is formed.

Q47. Why is Java considered partially (not purely) object-oriented?

Ans: Because it supports primitive data types (int, char, etc.) that are not objects, and static members

that do not need objects.

Q48. What are wrapper classes?

Ans: Classes such as Integer, Double and Boolean that wrap primitive values in objects so they can

be used in collections, generics and with null values.

Q49. What is autoboxing and unboxing?

Ans: Autoboxing is the automatic conversion of a primitive to its wrapper (int to Integer); unboxing is

the reverse. Unboxing a null wrapper throws NullPointerException.

Q50. What is the difference between == and equals()?

Ans: == compares primitive values or object references (identity). equals() compares logical

content when overridden, as in String and wrapper classes.

Section 2: Encapsulation and Access Modifiers

Q51. What is encapsulation?

Ans: Encapsulation is bundling data and the methods that operate on it into a single unit (class) and

restricting direct access to the data. In Java it is achieved with private fields and public getters/setters.

Q52. What are the benefits of encapsulation?

Ans: Data hiding, controlled access with validation, flexibility to change internals without affecting

callers, easier testing and maintenance, and improved security.

↑ Topic index
Book page 9

Java OOPs Concepts - 200 Interview Questions and Answers | Page 6

Q53. How do you achieve encapsulation in Java?

Ans: Declare fields private, expose them through public getter and setter methods, and put validation

logic in the setters.

Q54. What are access modifiers in Java?

Ans: Keywords controlling visibility: private (same class), default/package-private (same package),

protected (same package plus subclasses) and public (everywhere).

Q55. What is the default access modifier?

Ans: When no modifier is specified, the member has package-private access: visible only to classes

in the same package.

Q56. What is the difference between protected and default access?

Ans: Default access allows only the same package. Protected allows the same package and also

subclasses in other packages (through inheritance).

Q57. Can a top-level class be private or protected?

Ans: No. A top-level class can only be public or package-private. Nested classes can use all four

modifiers.

Q58. What is data hiding?

Ans: Preventing outside code from accessing an object's data directly, typically by marking fields

private so that access is only through controlled methods.

Q59. What is the difference between encapsulation and abstraction?

Ans: Abstraction hides complexity at the design level (what an object does); encapsulation hides data

at the implementation level (how it is protected and bundled). Abstraction is achieved via

interfaces/abstract classes, encapsulation via access modifiers.

Q60. What is a JavaBean?

Ans: A reusable class that follows conventions: a public no-arg constructor, private properties with

public getters/setters, and typically implements Serializable.

Q61. What is a POJO?

Ans: A Plain Old Java Object: a simple class not bound to any framework, extending no special class

and implementing no special interface, usually containing fields with getters/setters.

Q62. What is the difference between POJO and JavaBean?

Ans: Every JavaBean is a POJO, but a POJO need not follow bean conventions. JavaBeans must

have a no-arg constructor, be serializable and follow getter/setter naming.

Q63. Can encapsulation be broken in Java?

Ans: Yes, via reflection with setAccessible(true), or by returning references to mutable internal

objects from getters. Defensive copies and the module system reduce this risk.

Q64. What is a defensive copy?

Ans: Returning or storing a copy of a mutable object (like a Date or List) instead of the original

reference, so outside code cannot alter the internal state.

Q65. Why should fields be private?

Ans: To prevent invalid state, enable validation, allow internal changes without breaking clients and

support thread-safety strategies.

Q66. What is a read-only or write-only class?

Ans: A read-only class has only getters (no setters); a write-only class has only setters. Both are

achieved by choosing which accessors to expose.

Book page 10

Java OOPs Concepts - 200 Interview Questions and Answers | Page 7

Q67. What is the module system (JPMS) and how does it relate to encapsulation?

Ans: Introduced in Java 9, modules let you declare which packages are exported via

module-info.java. Non-exported packages are inaccessible even if public, giving stronger

encapsulation.

Section 3: Inheritance

Q68. What is inheritance?

Ans: A mechanism where a child (sub) class acquires the fields and methods of a parent (super)

class using the extends keyword, enabling code reuse and an IS-A relationship.

Q69. What are the types of inheritance in Java?

Ans: Single, multilevel and hierarchical inheritance are supported with classes. Multiple and hybrid

inheritance are achieved only through interfaces.

Q70. Why does Java not support multiple inheritance with classes?

Ans: To avoid the diamond problem, where ambiguity arises if two parent classes define the same

method, and to keep the language simpler.

Q71. What is the diamond problem?

Ans: When class D inherits from B and C, both of which inherit from A, and B and C override the

same method, D cannot decide which version to inherit. Java avoids this for classes and requires

explicit resolution for interface defaults.

Q72. How does Java achieve multiple inheritance?

Ans: Through interfaces: a class can implement many interfaces and an interface can extend multiple

interfaces.

Q73. What is the IS-A relationship?

Ans: The relationship expressed by inheritance: a Dog IS-A Animal. It is implemented with extends

(classes) or implements (interfaces).

Q74. What is the HAS-A relationship?

Ans: A relationship in which a class contains a reference to another class (composition or

aggregation), such as a Car HAS-A Engine.

Q75. What is composition and how does it differ from aggregation?

Ans: Both are HAS-A relationships. In composition the part cannot exist without the whole (strong

ownership, e.g. House and Room); in aggregation the part can exist independently (e.g. Team and

Player).

Q76. What is the difference between inheritance and composition?

Ans: Inheritance is IS-A, static and tightly coupled; composition is HAS-A, flexible and loosely

coupled. Modern design guidance is to favor composition over inheritance.

Q77. What is the super keyword?

Ans: A reference to the parent class. It is used to call the parent constructor super(...), access

hidden parent fields super.x, and invoke overridden parent methods super.method().

Q78. What is the root class of all Java classes?

Ans: java.lang.Object. Every class implicitly extends it if no other superclass is specified.

↑ Topic index
Book page 11

Java OOPs Concepts - 200 Interview Questions and Answers | Page 8

Q79. What members are not inherited by a subclass?

Ans: Private members are not accessible, constructors are not inherited, and package-private

members are not inherited by subclasses in other packages. Static members are inherited but are

hidden, not overridden.

Q80. Are constructors inherited?

Ans: No. A subclass must define its own constructors, which call a superclass constructor explicitly or

implicitly.

Q81. What happens if the parent class has no default constructor?

Ans: The subclass constructor must explicitly call a parent constructor with super(args); otherwise

the compiler raises an error because the implicit super() cannot be resolved.

Q82. Can a subclass access private members of its parent?

Ans: Not directly. It can access them only through public or protected getters/setters defined in the

parent.

Q83. What is the order of constructor execution in inheritance?

Ans: Parent constructors run before child constructors, from the top of the hierarchy down to the

actual class being instantiated.

Q84. Can we extend a final class?

Ans: No. A final class (such as String or Integer) cannot be subclassed.

Q85. What is the difference between extends and implements?

Ans: extends is used by a class to inherit from one class (or by an interface to extend interfaces);

implements is used by a class to adopt one or more interfaces.

Q86. Can a class extend and implement at the same time?

Ans: Yes. The extends clause must come first, then implements, e.g. class A extends B

implements C, D.

Q87. What is object type casting in inheritance?

Ans: Converting between parent and child reference types. Upcasting (child to parent) is implicit and

safe; downcasting (parent to child) requires an explicit cast and may throw ClassCastException.

Q88. What is the instanceof operator?

Ans: An operator that tests whether an object is an instance of a given class or interface, returning a

boolean. Java 16+ supports pattern matching: if (obj instanceof String s).

Q89. What is upcasting and downcasting?

Ans: Upcasting assigns a subclass object to a superclass reference (Animal a = new Dog()).

Downcasting converts it back (Dog d = (Dog) a), which should be guarded with instanceof.

Q90. What is method hiding?

Ans: When a subclass defines a static method with the same signature as a parent static method.

The method called depends on the reference type, not the object type.

Q91. What is variable hiding or shadowing?

Ans: When a subclass declares a field with the same name as a parent field. Field access is resolved

by the reference type at compile time, not by polymorphism.

Q92. What is the Liskov Substitution Principle?

Ans: Objects of a subclass must be usable wherever objects of the superclass are expected without

breaking program correctness. Overridden methods should honor the parent's contract.

Book page 12

Java OOPs Concepts - 200 Interview Questions and Answers | Page 9

Q93. Can an interface extend a class?

Ans: No. An interface can only extend other interfaces.

Q94. What is a marker interface?

Ans: An interface with no methods used to tag classes with a capability, such as Serializable,

Cloneable and RandomAccess.

Q95. What is the problem with deep inheritance hierarchies?

Ans: They create tight coupling, fragile base classes, difficulty understanding behavior and trouble

with changes. Prefer shallow hierarchies and composition.

Q96. What is the fragile base class problem?

Ans: A change in a parent class unintentionally breaks subclasses that depend on its implementation

details.

Q97. What is a sealed class (Java 17)?

Ans: A class or interface that restricts which classes may extend it using sealed and permits.

Subclasses must be final, sealed or non-sealed.

Section 4: Polymorphism and Method Overriding

Q98. What is polymorphism?

Ans: The ability of an entity to take many forms. In Java, the same method call can behave differently

based on the object it acts on. It is of two types: compile-time (overloading) and runtime (overriding).

Q99. What is compile-time polymorphism?

Ans: Also called static binding or early binding. Method overloading and operator behavior are

resolved by the compiler based on reference types and argument types.

Q100. What is runtime polymorphism?

Ans: Also called dynamic method dispatch. The JVM decides at runtime which overridden method to

call based on the actual object type, not the reference type.

Q101. What is method overriding?

Ans: When a subclass provides its own implementation of a method already defined in its superclass,

with the same name, parameters and a compatible return type.

Q102. What are the rules of method overriding?

Ans: Same name and parameter list; return type must be same or covariant; access level cannot be

more restrictive; cannot throw broader checked exceptions; cannot override final, static or private

methods.

Q103. What is the difference between overloading and overriding?

Ans: Overloading: same class, different parameters, resolved at compile time. Overriding:

parent-child classes, same signature, resolved at runtime.

Q104. What is dynamic method dispatch?

Ans: The process by which a call to an overridden method through a superclass reference is

resolved at runtime to the actual object's implementation.

Q105. What is a covariant return type?

Ans: An overriding method may return a subtype of the return type declared in the parent method,

e.g. parent returns Animal, child returns Dog.

↑ Topic index
Book page 13

Java OOPs Concepts - 200 Interview Questions and Answers | Page 10

Q106. What is the @Override annotation and why use it?

Ans: It tells the compiler that a method is intended to override a superclass method. The compiler

raises an error if no matching method exists, catching typos and signature mismatches.

Q107. Can we override a static method?

Ans: No. Static methods are bound to the class, so redefining one in a subclass is method hiding, not

overriding.

Q108. Can we override a private method?

Ans: No. Private methods are not visible to subclasses; a method with the same name in the

subclass is a completely new method.

Q109. Can we override a final method?

Ans: No. The compiler throws an error if a subclass tries to override a final method.

Q110. Can we reduce the visibility of an overridden method?

Ans: No. The overriding method must have the same or wider access. For example, a public method

cannot be overridden as protected.

Q111. What exceptions can an overriding method throw?

Ans: It can throw no exception, the same checked exception, a subclass of it, or any unchecked

exceptions. It cannot throw new or broader checked exceptions.

Q112. Can we override a method with a different return type?

Ans: Only if the new return type is covariant (a subtype) for reference types. Primitive return types

must match exactly.

Q113. What is early binding and late binding?

Ans: Early (static) binding is resolved at compile time for private, static, final methods and overloads.

Late (dynamic) binding is resolved at runtime for overridden instance methods.

Q114. Are fields polymorphic in Java?

Ans: No. Only instance methods are polymorphic. Field access depends on the reference type at

compile time.

Q115. What will be output if parent reference holds a child object and calls an overridden

method?

Ans: The child's version is executed because the JVM uses the actual object type at runtime. If the

method is not overridden, the parent's version runs.

Q116. Can a parent reference call a child-specific method?

Ans: Not directly. The reference type determines which methods are visible at compile time, so you

must downcast to the child type first.

Q117. What is the difference between static and dynamic binding?

Ans: Static binding uses type information at compile time and is faster; dynamic binding uses the

runtime object type and enables polymorphism.

Q118. Can constructors be overridden?

Ans: No. Constructors are not inherited, so they cannot be overridden, though they can be

overloaded.

Q119. How does the JVM implement dynamic dispatch internally?

Ans: Each class has a virtual method table (vtable) listing method implementations. At runtime the

JVM uses the object's class vtable to find the correct method.

↑ Topic index
Book page 14

Java OOPs Concepts - 200 Interview Questions and Answers | Page 11

Q120. Why is polymorphism useful?

Ans: It enables writing generic code against abstractions, reduces conditional logic, increases

extensibility and supports the open/closed principle.

Q121. What is parametric polymorphism?

Ans: Writing code that works with any type via generics, such as List<T>, providing type safety

without casting.

Section 5: Abstraction, Abstract Classes and Interfaces

Q122. What is abstraction?

Ans: The process of hiding implementation details and showing only essential functionality to the

user. In Java it is achieved with abstract classes and interfaces.

Q123. What is an abstract class?

Ans: A class declared with the abstract keyword that cannot be instantiated. It may contain

abstract methods (without body) and concrete methods, fields and constructors.

Q124. What is an abstract method?

Ans: A method declared without a body using the abstract keyword. Subclasses must implement it

unless they are also abstract.

Q125. Can an abstract class have a constructor?

Ans: Yes. It is called through super() when a concrete subclass object is created, and is used to

initialize the abstract class's fields.

Q126. Can an abstract class have no abstract methods?

Ans: Yes. Declaring it abstract simply prevents instantiation, which is useful for base classes meant

only to be extended.

Q127. Can we instantiate an abstract class?

Ans: No directly. We can only create objects of concrete subclasses, or use an anonymous subclass.

Q128. Can an abstract method be private, static or final?

Ans: No. These modifiers conflict with the need to override the method in subclasses.

Q129. Can an abstract class be final?

Ans: No. Final prevents extension, while abstract requires it, so the combination is a compile-time

error.

Q130. Can an abstract class implement an interface without defining its methods?

Ans: Yes. The unimplemented interface methods are inherited as abstract and must be implemented

by the first concrete subclass.

Q131. What is an interface?

Ans: A reference type that defines a contract of abstract methods (plus default, static and private

methods) that implementing classes must fulfil. Fields are implicitly public static final.

Q132. What are the features added to interfaces in Java 8 and 9?

Ans: Java 8 added default and static methods; Java 9 added private methods and private static

methods in interfaces.

Q133. What is a default method?

Ans: A method with a body in an interface, declared with default. It lets interfaces evolve without

breaking existing implementations.

↑ Topic index
Book page 15

Java OOPs Concepts - 200 Interview Questions and Answers | Page 12

Q134. What happens if two interfaces have the same default method?

Ans: The implementing class must override the method to resolve the conflict, optionally calling a

specific one using InterfaceName.super.method().

Q135. Can an interface have a static method?

Ans: Yes, since Java 8. It is called using the interface name and is not inherited by implementing

classes.

Q136. Can an interface have a constructor?

Ans: No. Interfaces cannot be instantiated and have no instance state, so constructors are not

allowed.

Q137. Can interfaces have variables?

Ans: Yes, but they are implicitly public static final constants and must be initialized at

declaration.

Q138. What is a functional interface?

Ans: An interface with exactly one abstract method, usable as a lambda target. It may be annotated

with @FunctionalInterface, e.g. Runnable, Comparator, Function.

Q139. What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface?

Ans: An abstract class can hold state, constructors and any access modifiers and allows single

inheritance. An interface defines a contract, has constants only, supports multiple inheritance and is

used for unrelated classes.

Q140. When should you use an abstract class over an interface?

Ans: When classes share common state or code and are closely related; use an interface to define a

capability that unrelated classes can implement.

Q141. Can an interface extend multiple interfaces?

Ans: Yes. An interface can extend any number of interfaces using comma-separated names.

Q142. Are all interface methods public?

Ans: Yes. Abstract, default and static interface methods are implicitly public; only private methods

(Java 9+) are non-public.

Q143. Can a class implement multiple interfaces having the same method signature?

Ans: Yes, and a single implementation satisfies both. If return types conflict, compilation fails.

Q144. What is a tagging or marker interface used for?

Ans: It signals metadata to the JVM or libraries, e.g. Serializable tells the serialization mechanism an

object can be persisted.

Q145. Can an interface be final?

Ans: No. An interface exists to be implemented, so final contradicts its purpose.

Section 6: Nested and Inner Classes, Enums, Records

Q146. What is a nested class?

Ans: A class defined inside another class. Types are static nested classes and inner (non-static)

classes, which include member, local and anonymous classes.

Q147. What is an inner class?

Ans: A non-static nested class that is associated with an instance of the outer class and can access

all its members, including private ones.

↑ Topic index
Book page 16

Java OOPs Concepts - 200 Interview Questions and Answers | Page 13

Q148. What is a static nested class?

Ans: A nested class declared static. It does not need an outer instance and can access only the

outer class's static members directly.

Q149. What is the difference between inner class and static nested class?

Ans: An inner class holds an implicit reference to an outer instance; a static nested class does not

and can be instantiated independently.

Q150. What is a local class?

Ans: A class declared inside a method or block. It is visible only within that scope and can use

effectively final local variables.

Q151. What is an anonymous class?

Ans: A nameless class declared and instantiated in a single expression, typically to implement an

interface or extend a class on the spot.

Q152. How do you instantiate an inner class from outside?

Ans: Outer.Inner in = new Outer().new Inner();. For static nested classes, use new

Outer.Nested().

Q153. Why must local variables used in an inner class or lambda be effectively final?

Ans: Because the inner object may outlive the method call and holds a copy of the value. Requiring

effective finality avoids inconsistent copies.

Q154. What is the difference between an anonymous class and a lambda?

Ans: An anonymous class creates a new type with its own this and can implement any interface or

class; a lambda works only for functional interfaces, this refers to the enclosing class, and it is more

concise.

Q155. What is an enum in Java?

Ans: A special class representing a fixed set of constants. Enums can have fields, constructors and

methods, implicitly extend java.lang.Enum and are type-safe.

Q156. Can an enum extend a class or implement an interface?

Ans: It cannot extend a class (it already extends Enum) but it can implement interfaces.

Q157. Can we create an enum instance using new?

Ans: No. Enum constructors are implicitly private and constants are created by the JVM at class

loading.

Q158. What is a record in Java (Java 16+)?

Ans: A concise immutable data carrier class declared with record Point(int x, int y) {}.

The compiler generates the constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString.

Q159. Can a record extend another class?

Ans: No. Records implicitly extend java.lang.Record and are final, but they can implement

interfaces.

Section 7: Object Class, Immutability and Core Methods

Q160. What are the main methods of the Object class?

Ans: equals, hashCode, toString, clone, finalize, getClass, notify, notifyAll and

wait (three overloads).

↑ Topic index
Book page 17

Java OOPs Concepts - 200 Interview Questions and Answers | Page 14

Q161. What is the contract between equals() and hashCode()?

Ans: If two objects are equal by equals(), they must return the same hashCode(). Unequal

objects may share a hashcode, but good hashing reduces collisions.

Q162. What happens if you override equals() but not hashCode()?

Ans: Hash-based collections like HashMap and HashSet may behave incorrectly, as equal objects

can land in different buckets and become unfindable.

Q163. What is the default implementation of toString()?

Ans: It returns the class name, an @ sign and the hexadecimal hashcode, e.g.

Employee@1b6d3586. It is usually overridden for readable output.

Q164. What is the clone() method?

Ans: A protected Object method that creates a copy of an object. The class must implement the

Cloneable interface or CloneNotSupportedException is thrown.

Q165. What is the difference between shallow copy and deep copy?

Ans: A shallow copy duplicates the object but shares referenced objects; a deep copy duplicates the

object and recursively copies all referenced objects.

Q166. How can you create an immutable class?

Ans: Declare the class final, make all fields private and final, provide no setters, initialize via the

constructor, and use defensive copies for mutable fields.

Q167. Why is String immutable?

Ans: For security, thread safety, caching of hashcodes, String pool memory optimization and safe

use as map keys.

Q168. What is the String pool?

Ans: A special area of the heap where string literals are stored and reused. intern() places or

retrieves a string from the pool.

Q169. What is the difference between String, StringBuilder and StringBuffer?

Ans: String is immutable; StringBuilder is mutable and not thread-safe (faster); StringBuffer is

mutable and synchronized (thread-safe).

Q170. What is getClass() and how does it differ from instanceof?

Ans: getClass() returns the exact runtime class; instanceof also returns true for subclasses

and implemented interfaces.

Q171. What is reflection?

Ans: An API (java.lang.reflect) to inspect and modify classes, methods and fields at runtime,

even private ones. It is powerful but slower and can break encapsulation.

Q172. What is the singleton design pattern?

Ans: A pattern ensuring a class has only one instance with a global access point. It uses a private

constructor and a static accessor, with thread-safe options such as an enum or holder class.

Q173. How do you make a singleton thread-safe?

Ans: Use eager initialization, a synchronized method, double-checked locking with volatile, the

Bill Pugh holder idiom or a single-element enum.

Q174. Can reflection or serialization break a singleton?

Ans: Yes. Reflection can call the private constructor and deserialization can create a new instance.

Enum singletons are immune to both.

↑ Topic index
Book page 18

Java OOPs Concepts - 200 Interview Questions and Answers | Page 15

Q175. What is the Comparable vs Comparator difference?

Ans: Comparable defines natural ordering inside the class via compareTo; Comparator defines

external, custom ordering via compare and allows multiple sort strategies.

Q176. What is serialization?

Ans: Converting an object's state into a byte stream to store or transmit it. A class must implement

Serializable; transient fields are skipped and serialVersionUID versions the class.

Q177. What is the transient keyword?

Ans: It marks a field to be excluded from serialization, so it takes its default value on deserialization.

Section 8: Design Principles, Patterns and Advanced Concepts

Q178. What are the SOLID principles?

Ans: Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation and

Dependency Inversion: five guidelines for maintainable object-oriented design.

Q179. What is the Single Responsibility Principle?

Ans: A class should have only one reason to change, meaning it should do one job.

Q180. What is the Open/Closed Principle?

Ans: Classes should be open for extension but closed for modification, typically achieved through

abstraction and polymorphism.

Q181. What is the Interface Segregation Principle?

Ans: Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use; prefer several small,

specific interfaces over one large one.

Q182. What is the Dependency Inversion Principle?

Ans: High-level modules should depend on abstractions, not on concrete low-level modules.

Dependency injection is a common way to apply it.

Q183. What is coupling and cohesion?

Ans: Coupling is how strongly classes depend on each other; cohesion is how closely a class's

responsibilities relate. Good design has low coupling and high cohesion.

Q184. What is dependency injection?

Ans: A technique where an object receives its dependencies from outside (constructor, setter or field)

instead of creating them, improving testability and loose coupling.

Q185. What is the factory design pattern?

Ans: A creational pattern that provides a method to create objects without exposing instantiation

logic, returning instances through a common interface.

Q186. What is the Builder pattern?

Ans: A creational pattern that constructs complex objects step by step with a fluent API, helpful when

there are many optional parameters.

Q187. What is the Strategy pattern?

Ans: A behavioral pattern that defines a family of interchangeable algorithms behind an interface and

lets clients switch them at runtime, an application of polymorphism.

Q188. What is the difference between association, aggregation and composition?

Ans: Association is a general relationship between classes; aggregation is a weak HAS-A where

parts exist independently; composition is a strong HAS-A where parts die with the owner.

↑ Topic index
Book page 19

Java OOPs Concepts - 200 Interview Questions and Answers | Page 16

Q189. What is a generic class and why use generics?

Ans: A class parameterized with types, like Box<T>. Generics give compile-time type safety,

eliminate casts and enable reusable code.

Q190. What is type erasure?

Ans: The compiler removes generic type information after checking, replacing type parameters with

their bounds (or Object), so generics do not exist at runtime.

Q191. What is the difference between ? extends T and ? super T?

Ans: ? extends T is an upper-bounded wildcard for reading (producer); ? super T is a

lower-bounded wildcard for writing (consumer): the PECS rule.

Q192. What are the advantages of OOP?

Ans: Code reusability, modularity, easier maintenance, data security via encapsulation, scalability,

flexibility through polymorphism and natural modeling of real-world problems.

Q193. What are the disadvantages of OOP?

Ans: Greater design complexity, more memory and CPU overhead, steeper learning curve, and a risk

of over-engineering or deep hierarchies for simple problems.

Q194. What is the difference between procedural and object-oriented programming?

Ans: Procedural programming is function-centric, top-down and exposes data globally; OOP is

object-centric, bottom-up and protects data through encapsulation.

Q195. What is a memory leak in Java and how can it relate to OOP?

Ans: It occurs when unused objects remain reachable and cannot be collected, such as static

collections holding references, unclosed listeners or inner classes retaining outer instances.

Q196. What does it mean to program to an interface, not an implementation?

Ans: Declare variables and parameters with interface types (e.g. List<String> list = new

ArrayList<>()) so implementations can be swapped without changing client code.

Q197. What is a copy constructor and why is it preferred over clone()?

Ans: A constructor that takes an object of the same class and copies its fields. It is type-safe, simpler

and avoids the pitfalls of Cloneable.

Q198. Can we have multiple classes in one Java file?

Ans: Yes, but at most one can be public and its name must match the file name. Other classes are

package-private.

Q199. What is the significance of the serialVersionUID?

Ans: A version identifier for Serializable classes. During deserialization the JVM compares it with the

stored one and throws InvalidClassException if they differ.

Q200. What are the best practices for writing good OOP code in Java?

Ans: Favor composition over inheritance, keep fields private, program to interfaces, make classes

immutable where possible, follow SOLID, keep classes small and cohesive, and override

equals/hashCode/toString consistently.
