Section 1: Generics Fundamentals

Q1. What are generics in Java?

Generics let classes, interfaces and methods operate on types that are specified as parameters, e.g.

List<String>. They provide compile-time type safety and remove the need for most explicit casts.

Q2. In which Java version were generics introduced, and why?

Java 5 (2004). They were added to catch type errors at compile time instead of runtime

ClassCastExceptions, and to make collection code more readable and reusable.

Q3. What are the main benefits of generics?

Compile-time type checking, elimination of casts, code reuse through type-parameterized algorithms,

and self-documenting APIs (the type states what a collection holds).

Q4. What is the syntax for declaring a generic class?

class Box<T> { private T value; T get() { return value; } void set(T v) {

value = v; } }. The type parameter list goes in angle brackets after the class name.

Q5. How do you declare a generic interface?

interface Repository<T, ID> { T findById(ID id); }. Implementers either supply

concrete types (class UserRepo implements Repository<User, Long>) or stay generic.

Q6. What are the standard naming conventions for type parameters?

Single uppercase letters: T (type), E (element), K (key), V (value), N (number), and S, U, V for second,

third, fourth types.

Q7. Can primitives be used as type arguments?

No. List<int> is illegal because type arguments must be reference types. Use wrappers such as

List<Integer>; autoboxing handles conversion.

Q8. What is the diamond operator?

The <> syntax (Java 7) that lets the compiler infer type arguments on the right-hand side:

Map<String, List<Integer>> m = new HashMap<>();.

Q9. What is a raw type?

A generic class or interface used without type arguments, such as List instead of List<String>. It

exists for backward compatibility with pre-Java 5 code.

Q10. Why should raw types be avoided?

They bypass generic type checking, so errors surface as runtime ClassCastExceptions, and they

produce unchecked warnings. All generic members of a raw type are also erased.

Q11. What is an unchecked warning?

A compiler warning that type safety cannot be verified at compile time, typically from raw-type use or an

unchecked cast like (List<String>) obj.

Q12. When is it acceptable to use @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")?

Only when you can prove the operation is type-safe, applied to the smallest possible scope (a single

declaration), with a comment explaining why it is safe.

↑ Topic index
Book page 22

Java Generics & Invariance - 200 Interview Questions

Page 3

Q13. How do generics differ from using Object everywhere?

With Object you need manual casts and errors appear at runtime. Generics move type checking to

compile time and the compiler inserts the casts for you.

Q14. Can a class have multiple type parameters?

Yes: class Pair<K, V> { K key; V value; }. Separate them with commas.

Q15. Can a constructor be generic?

Yes. A constructor can declare its own type parameters: class A { <T> A(T t) { } }, even

inside a non-generic class.

Q16. What is the difference between a type parameter and a type argument?

A type parameter is the placeholder in a declaration (T in class Box<T>). A type argument is the

concrete type supplied on use (String in Box<String>).

Q17. What is a parameterized type?

A generic type invoked with actual type arguments, such as List<String> or Map<String,

Integer>.

Q18. Why can't you write new T()?

Because of type erasure, T is not known at runtime, so the JVM cannot instantiate it. Workarounds:

pass a Class<T> and use reflection, or pass a Supplier<T>.

Q19. Why can't you create a generic array like new T[10]?

Arrays are reified (they know their component type at runtime) while T is erased, so the array's runtime

type cannot be determined safely. Use (T[]) new Object[10] with care, or

Array.newInstance.

Q20. Can a static field have a type parameter type?

No. Static members are shared across all parameterizations of the class, so static T value; would

have no single meaning for Box<String> and Box<Integer>.

Q21. Do List<String> and List<Integer> have different runtime classes?

No. Both are just ArrayList (or whatever the implementation is) at runtime; list1.getClass() ==

list2.getClass() is true due to erasure.

Q22. Can you use instanceof with a parameterized type?

Not with a non-reifiable type: obj instanceof List<String> is a compile error when the check

cannot be verified. obj instanceof List<?> is allowed.

Q23. Can a generic class extend Throwable?

No. The JVM catches exceptions by runtime type, which erasure would make ambiguous, so class

MyEx<T> extends Exception is illegal.

Q24. Can you catch a type parameter, e.g. catch (T e)?

No, for the same erasure reason. However, a type parameter may appear in a throws clause: <E

extends Exception> void run() throws E.

Q25. How does inheritance work with generic classes?

A subclass can pass its type parameter up (class Sub<T> extends Base<T>) or fix it (class

IntBox extends Box<Integer>). It can also add new type parameters.

↑ Topic index
Book page 23

Java Generics & Invariance - 200 Interview Questions

Page 4

Q26. How do autoboxing and generics interact?

With List<Integer>, list.add(5) boxes the int automatically and int x = list.get(0)

unboxes it. Unboxing a null element throws NullPointerException.

Q27. Can a static method use the class's type parameter?

No. A static method must declare its own type parameters: static <T> Box<T> of(T v). The

class-level T belongs to instances.

Q28. How would you implement a simple generic Pair<A, B>?

final class Pair<A, B> { private final A first; private final B second;

Pair(A a, B b) {...} A first() {...} B second() {...} }, or simply record

Pair<A, B>(A first, B second) {} in Java 16+.

Q29. How has type argument inference evolved across Java versions?

Java 5 inferred only for method arguments; Java 7 added the diamond; Java 8 added target typing for

poly expressions and lambdas; Java 9 allowed diamond with anonymous classes; Java 10 added var

for locals.

Q30. What is a generic method?

A method with its own type parameters declared before the return type: static <T> T

first(List<T> list).

Q31. Is the type parameter of a class in scope inside its nested static class?

No. A static nested class cannot reference the outer class's type parameters; an inner (non-static) class

can.

Section 2: Bounds and Wildcards

Q32. What is a bounded type parameter?

A type parameter restricted to a type or its subtypes: <T extends Number>. It lets you call Number

methods on T.

Q33. How do you specify multiple bounds?

Use &: <T extends Number & Comparable<T>>. The type argument must satisfy all bounds.

Q34. In multiple bounds, which bound must come first?

If one bound is a class, it must be listed first; the rest must be interfaces. <T extends Runnable &

Number> is a compile error.

Q35. What is a recursive (F-bounded) type bound?

A bound that refers to the type parameter itself: <T extends Comparable<T>>. It says "T can be

compared to other Ts".

Q36. Why does Collections.sort use <T extends Comparable<? super T>>?

So that a type can be sorted if it inherits Comparable from a supertype. E.g. java.sql.Timestamp

extends Date, which implements Comparable<Date>, not Comparable<Timestamp>.

Q37. What is a wildcard in Java generics?

The ? symbol, representing an unknown type argument. It is used at the use site, e.g. List<?>,

List<? extends Number>, List<? super Integer>.

↑ Topic index
Book page 24

Java Generics & Invariance - 200 Interview Questions

Page 5

Q38. What is an upper-bounded wildcard?

? extends X means "some unknown type that is X or a subtype of X". It makes the type covariant

and is mainly for reading.

Q39. What is a lower-bounded wildcard?

? super X means "some unknown type that is X or a supertype of X". It makes the type contravariant

and is mainly for writing.

Q40. When do you use an unbounded wildcard?

When the code works with the structure and not the element type, e.g. void

printSize(Collection<?> c) or Class<?>.

Q41. What is the difference between List<?> and List<Object>?

List<Object> is a list that accepts any object and is not a supertype relative to List<String>.

List<?> is a list of one unknown type and is a supertype of every List<X>, but you cannot add

elements to it (except null).

Q42. Can you add elements to a List<?>?

Only null. The compiler doesn't know the actual element type, so no other value is provably safe.

Q43. Can you add elements to a List<? extends Number>?

Only null. The list could really be List<Integer> or List<Double>, so adding a Number or

Integer is not safe.

Q44. Can you add elements to a List<? super Integer>?

Yes, you can add Integer (and its subtypes), because whatever the actual list type is, it can hold

Integers.

Q45. What can you read from a List<? super Integer>?

Only Object, since the element type could be any supertype of Integer.

Q46. What does PECS stand for?

"Producer Extends, Consumer Super" (Joshua Bloch). If a parameter produces values you read, use ?

extends T; if it consumes values you write, use ? super T.

Q47. What does the signature of Collections.copy look like and why?

static <T> void copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src). The source

produces (extends), the destination consumes (super).

Q48. What is wildcard capture?

When the compiler gives a fresh, anonymous type variable (e.g. CAP#1) to a wildcard so it can

type-check an operation. It appears in error messages like "incompatible types: Object cannot be

converted to CAP#1".

Q49. What is a capture helper method?

A private generic method that captures a wildcard into a named type variable: void swap(List<?>

l) { swapHelper(l); } private <T> void swapHelper(List<T> l) { T t =

l.get(0); l.set(0, l.get(1)); l.set(1, t); }.

↑ Topic index
Book page 25

Java Generics & Invariance - 200 Interview Questions

Page 6

Q50. Why can't you write list.set(0, list.get(1)) directly on a List<?>?

The two uses of ? capture different unknown types, so the compiler can't prove the value fits. A helper

with a named type parameter solves it.

Q51. When should you use a type parameter <T> rather than a wildcard?

Use <T> when the type is needed more than once (relating parameters or return type) or when you

need to refer to it in the body. Use a wildcard when the type appears once and isn't referenced.

Q52. Can a wildcard be used in a class declaration?

No. Wildcards are only for type arguments at use sites; a declaration like class Foo<?> is illegal.

Q53. Can you instantiate a class with a wildcard, like new ArrayList<?>()?

No. Wildcards can't be used as top-level type arguments in a new expression, though new

ArrayList<List<?>>() is legal.

Q54. What is Class<?>?

A Class object whose represented type is unknown. It is the safe way to write "any class" without

using the raw Class type.

Q55. What does Class<? extends Number> allow?

Any class literal whose type is Number or a subclass: Integer.class, Double.class, etc.

Q56. Should you use wildcard types as return types?

Generally no (Effective Java Item 31). They force callers to deal with wildcards. Use them for

parameters, and return a concrete parameterized type.

Q57. What is an intersection type?

A type that is a subtype of several types at once, appearing as A & B in multiple bounds or in inferred

types, e.g. the inferred type of List.of(1, "a") elements is Object & Serializable &

Comparable<...> & Constable....

Q58. Can you write a lower bound on a type parameter, like <T super Integer>?

No. Java supports lower bounds only on wildcards (? super Integer), not on type parameters.

Q59. What is the difference between void f(List<? extends T> l) and void f(List<T>

l)?

The first accepts a list of T or any subtype of T (read-only usage); the second accepts only List<T>

exactly, allowing both reads and writes.

Q60. What is Enum<E extends Enum<E>> and why is it declared that way?

It's an F-bound ensuring each enum type is Enum of itself, so methods like compareTo(E o) accept

only the same enum type.

Q61. What are self-bounded generics (CRTP-style)?

A pattern like abstract class Builder<T extends Builder<T>> { abstract T self();

} where subclasses pass themselves, enabling fluent APIs that return the subclass type.

Q62. How do self-bounded generics help the Builder pattern?

Base-class methods can return T (the concrete builder), so chained calls keep subclass methods

available: new CarBuilder().color("red").wheels(4).

↑ Topic index
Book page 26

Java Generics & Invariance - 200 Interview Questions

Page 7

Q63. Why does Collections.sort(List<T>, Comparator<? super T>) use ? super T?

A comparator for a supertype can compare subtypes. A Comparator<Object> can sort a

List<String>.

Q64. Explain Function<? super T, ? extends R> in stream APIs.

The function consumes T (so accepting a function on a supertype is fine) and produces R (so a

function returning a subtype is fine). That's PECS applied to functional interfaces.

Q65. What is the signature of Stream.map and why?

<R> Stream<R> map(Function<? super T, ? extends R> mapper). It maximizes flexibility

for callers, who may pass functions defined on supertypes or returning subtypes.

Q66. Why does Optional.orElseGet take Supplier<? extends T>?

The supplier produces values, so a supplier of any subtype of T is acceptable.

Q67. Is List<List<?>> the same as List<? extends List<?>>?

No. List<List<?>> is a list whose elements are lists of anything (you can add any List<?>).

List<? extends List<?>> could be a List<ArrayList<String>>, so you can't add anything.

Q68. Can a wildcard bound refer to a type variable?

Yes: <T> void addAll(Collection<? extends T> src, Collection<? super T> dst).

Q69. Is List<? extends Object> the same as List<?>?

Effectively yes; an unbounded wildcard is equivalent to ? extends Object.

Q70. What does it mean to say that ? is not a type?

A wildcard is not a type itself but a placeholder for an unknown type argument; you cannot declare a

variable of type ? or use it as a standalone type.

Q71. Can a wildcard have both an upper and lower bound?

No. Java permits either ? extends X or ? super X, not both on the same wildcard.

Q72. What happens if you try to read a T from a Map<String, ? extends Number>?

get returns Number (the upper bound), which is safe. But put(key, value) is rejected for every

non-null value.

Q73. How do you write a method that sums a list of any Number subtype?

static double sum(Collection<? extends Number> c) { double s = 0; for

(Number n : c) s += n.doubleValue(); return s; }.

Q74. How do you write a method that fills a list with Integers, accepting List<Integer>,

List<Number>, or List<Object>?

static void fill(List<? super Integer> list) { for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++)

list.add(i); }.

Q75. How would you declare a generic method that returns the max of a collection?

static <T extends Object & Comparable<? super T>> T max(Collection<? extends

T> c), which mirrors Collections.max.

↑ Topic index
Book page 27

Java Generics & Invariance - 200 Interview Questions

Page 8

Q76. Why does Collections.max use T extends Object & Comparable<? super T>?

To keep the erasure of T as Object for binary compatibility with pre-generics code, while still requiring

Comparable.

Q77. What does ? super T allow in a Predicate?

Predicate<? super T> accepts predicates defined for T or any supertype, e.g. a

Predicate<Object> can filter a Stream<String>.

Q78. Can a method parameter type be List<? extends Number>[]?

Yes, arrays of wildcard-parameterized types with unbounded wildcards are allowed, but with bounded

wildcards (List<? extends Number>[]) creation is illegal while declaration is fine.

Section 3: Invariance, Covariance and Contravariance

Q79. What is invariance in Java generics?

Parameterized types are invariant in their type arguments: List<String> is not a subtype of

List<Object>, even though String is a subtype of Object.

Q80. Is List<Object> a supertype of List<String>?

No. They are unrelated types. List<Object> lo = new ArrayList<String>(); doesn't

compile.

Q81. Why are generics invariant?

To preserve type safety. If List<String> were a List<Object>, you could add an Integer

through the Object view and later get a ClassCastException reading it as String.

Q82. Give a code example that shows why generic invariance is needed.

List<String> ls = new ArrayList<>(); List<Object> lo = ls; lo.add(42);

String s = ls.get(0); would crash at the last line if the second line were legal. The compiler

rejects the second line.

Q83. Are arrays covariant or invariant in Java?

Covariant: String[] is a subtype of Object[]. This is checked at runtime, not compile time.

Q84. What happens in Object[] a = new String[1]; a[0] = 1;?

It compiles, but throws ArrayStoreException at runtime because the actual array is a String[].

Q85. What is the key difference between arrays and generics regarding type safety?

Arrays are covariant and reified (errors at runtime). Generics are invariant and erased (errors at

compile time). This mismatch is why you can't create generic arrays.

Q86. What is covariance?

If B is a subtype of A, then Producer<B> is a subtype of Producer<A>. In Java this is expressed with

? extends: List<Integer> is a List<? extends Number>.

Q87. What is contravariance?

If B is a subtype of A, then Consumer<A> is a subtype of Consumer<B>. In Java this is expressed with

? super: List<Number> is a List<? super Integer>.

↑ Topic index
Book page 28

Java Generics & Invariance - 200 Interview Questions

Page 9

Q88. What is bivariance and does Java support it?

Bivariance would let a type be treated as both co- and contravariant. Java doesn't support it; the

unbounded wildcard ? is the closest idea, but with strong restrictions.

Q89. How do you achieve covariance with generics in Java?

Use an upper-bounded wildcard at the use site: List<? extends Number> nums = new

ArrayList<Integer>();.

Q90. How do you achieve contravariance with generics in Java?

Use a lower-bounded wildcard at the use site: List<? super Integer> sink = new

ArrayList<Number>();.

Q91. What is the subtyping relation among wildcard types?

List<Integer> is a subtype of List<? extends Integer>, which is a subtype of List<?

extends Number>, which is a subtype of List<?>. For super: List<Number> is a subtype of

List<? super Integer>, which is a subtype of List<? super IntegerSubtype>.

Q92. Is ArrayList<String> a subtype of List<String>?

Yes. Invariance only concerns type arguments. Subtyping between the generic class types themselves

(ArrayList extends AbstractList implements List) is preserved when the type argument is the

same.

Q93. Why does List<Number> nums = new ArrayList<Integer>(); fail?

Because ArrayList<Integer> is not a List<Number> due to invariance.

Q94. How do you fix List<Number> nums = new ArrayList<Integer>();?

Declare the variable with a wildcard: List<? extends Number> nums = new

ArrayList<Integer>();. You can then read Numbers but not add to it.

Q95. Why can't you write to a covariant view such as List<? extends Number>?

The real list might be List<Integer>, and adding a Double would corrupt it. The compiler can't

know, so it prohibits all adds except null.

Q96. Why can you only read Object from a contravariant view such as List<? super

Integer>?

The actual list might be List<Object> or List<Number>, so the only guaranteed upper type of its

elements is Object.

Q97. Does Java allow covariant return types in overriding?

Yes (Java 5+). An overriding method may return a subtype: Object clone() can be overridden as

MyType clone(). The compiler adds a bridge method.

Q98. Are method parameter types covariant when overriding?

No, they must match exactly. Changing the parameter type creates an overload, not an override. This

is parameter invariance.

Q99. What happens when a subclass method has a generic parameter that differs from the

parent's?

void f(List<String>) in a subclass of a class with void f(List<Object>) is neither an

override nor a valid overload when erasures clash, producing a name clash error.

↑ Topic index
Book page 29

Java Generics & Invariance - 200 Interview Questions

Page 10

Q100. Can a generic method be overridden?

Yes, if the signatures have the same type parameters (same number and bounds) and the same

parameter types after renaming.

Q101. Is Comparable<Number> implemented by Integer?

No. Integer implements Comparable<Integer>. That's why APIs use Comparable<? super T>

to remain flexible.

Q102. Why is Comparable<? super T> a contravariant use?

Comparable<X> consumes an X in compareTo(X). A comparable on a supertype of T can safely

compare Ts.

Q103. Can you assign Function<Object, String> to Function<? super String, ?

extends CharSequence>?

Yes. The function accepts Object (a supertype of String) and returns String (a subtype of

CharSequence).

Q104. Is Consumer<Object> a subtype of Consumer<String>?

No, generics are invariant. But a Consumer<Object> can be passed where Consumer<? super

String> is expected.

Q105. What is declaration-site variance versus use-site variance?

Declaration-site variance fixes variance on the type definition (Kotlin out T, C# out T). Use-site

variance specifies it at each usage with wildcards. Java uses use-site variance.

Q106. How does Java's ? extends compare to Kotlin's out?

Kotlin's List<out T> is declared covariant once for all uses; in Java, each use must write List<?

extends T>. Kotlin also supports use-site projections similar to Java's.

Q107. How does Java's ? super compare to Kotlin's in?

Same idea: Comparator<in T> in Kotlin corresponds to Comparator<? super T> in Java.

Q108. Why did Java choose use-site variance?

Java interfaces like List both read and write T, so they can't be soundly covariant or contravariant

across the board. Use-site variance lets one type serve all roles.

Q109. What is heap pollution?

A situation where a variable of a parameterized type refers to an object that is not of that parameterized

type, e.g. through raw types or unchecked casts.

Q110. Show an example of heap pollution leading to ClassCastException.

List raw = new ArrayList<String>(); raw.add(1); List<String> ls = raw;

String s = ls.get(0); compiles with warnings and fails at the last line.

Q111. Why can Collections.unmodifiableList accept List<? extends T> and return

List<T>?

The returned list is read-only, so exposing it as the more general List<T> can't be abused by writes.

Q112. How does Collections.emptyList() work with inference?

It's static <T> List<T> emptyList(), and the compiler infers T from the assignment target:

List<String> l = Collections.emptyList();.

↑ Topic index
Book page 30

Java Generics & Invariance - 200 Interview Questions

Page 11

Q113. Is List<? extends Number> assignable to List<?>?

Yes. List<?> is a supertype of every parameterization.

Q114. Is List<?> a supertype of all List<X>?

Yes, List<?> (equivalent to List<? extends Object>) is the common supertype of all

parameterizations of List.

Q115. Does List<Number> l = List.of(1, 2.0); compile?

Yes. The target type drives inference, so E is inferred as Number, and the Integer and Double

arguments are compatible.

Q116. Why can't you create new List<String>[10]?

Because arrays are covariant and reified, generic arrays would allow heap pollution without runtime

ArrayStoreException protection.

Q117. Show how generic arrays could break type safety if allowed.

List<String>[] ls = new List<String>[1]; Object[] o = ls; o[0] = new

ArrayList<Integer>(); String s = ls[0].get(0); would fail with ClassCastException

and no ArrayStoreException.

Q118. What are workarounds for generic array creation?

Use List<List<String>>, use an array of unbounded wildcards (List<?>[]), use

Array.newInstance, or cast (List<String>[]) new List[10] with

@SuppressWarnings("unchecked").

Q119. What does @SafeVarargs do?

It suppresses unchecked warnings for generic varargs methods whose body doesn't misuse the implicit

array. It asserts that the method doesn't write to or expose the varargs array.

Q120. On which methods can @SafeVarargs be applied?

Constructors, and static, final, and (since Java 9) private methods; not on ordinary overridable

instance methods.

Q121. Is Map<String, List<Integer>> a subtype of Map<String, List<? extends

Number>>?

No, because of invariance on the second type argument: List<Integer> is not the same type as

List<? extends Number>.

Q122. How do you fix the nested case Map<String, List<Integer>> to Map<String,

List<? extends Number>>?

Use a wildcard at the outer level too: Map<String, ? extends List<? extends Number>>.

Q123. What are the type-argument containment rules?

T <= ? extends S if T <: S; T <= ? super S if S <: T; and any type argument is contained in

?. A parameterized type G<A> is a subtype of G<B> only if A is contained by B.

Q124. Is Class<Integer> assignable to Class<? extends Number>?

Yes, because Integer is a subtype of Number and the wildcard is covariant.

Section 4: Type Erasure and Reifiability

↑ Topic index
Book page 31

Java Generics & Invariance - 200 Interview Questions

Page 12

Q125. What is type erasure?

The compiler process that removes type parameters and arguments after type checking. It replaces

type variables by their bounds (or Object), inserts casts, and generates bridge methods where

needed.

Q126. What are the rules of type erasure?

An unbounded type variable erases to Object; a bounded one erases to its leftmost bound;

parameterized types erase to their raw type; the compiler inserts casts and bridge methods.

Q127. Why did Java implement generics with erasure?

To keep migration compatibility: old and new code could interoperate and the JVM and class file format

didn't need a breaking change.

Q128. What are bridge methods?

Synthetic methods generated by the compiler to preserve polymorphism after erasure or covariant

returns. E.g. class A implements Comparable<A> gets a synthetic compareTo(Object) that

casts and delegates to compareTo(A).

Q129. When does a compiler generate a bridge method?

When overriding or implementing a generic method with a specific type, or using a covariant return

type, so the erased signature still matches the parent's.

Q130. What is a reifiable type?

A type whose runtime representation carries full type information. Reifiable types include primitives,

non-generic types, raw types, unbounded wildcard parameterizations like List<?>, and arrays of

reifiable types.

Q131. Which types are non-reifiable?

Type variables (T), parameterized types with concrete arguments (List<String>), and

parameterized types with bounded wildcards (List<? extends Number>).

Q132. Why is obj instanceof List<String> illegal?

The JVM can't check the type argument at runtime because it's erased. Only List<?> or raw List

can be tested.

Q133. Is obj instanceof List<?> legal?

Yes, since List<?> is reifiable. It is functionally the same as obj instanceof List.

Q134. What happens when you cast (List<String>) obj?

It compiles with an unchecked warning. At runtime only the raw class List is checked, so a wrong

element type will surface later as a ClassCastException.

Q135. Can you overload void f(List<String>) and void f(List<Integer>)?

No. After erasure both become f(List), causing a "name clash: same erasure" compile error.

Q136. What is a "name clash" error?

A compile error indicating that two methods have the same signature after erasure, or an override fails

to match due to erasure differences.

↑ Topic index
Book page 32

Java Generics & Invariance - 200 Interview Questions

Page 13

Q137. Can generic type information be obtained at runtime?

Partially. Class files keep generic signatures for declarations (fields, method signatures, supertypes),

accessible via reflection such as getGenericSuperclass() and getGenericReturnType().

Local variables and instance type arguments are lost.

Q138. What is a super type token?

A technique that captures a generic type by creating an anonymous subclass, e.g. new

TypeReference<List<String>>() {}, then reading getGenericSuperclass() to recover the

actual type argument.

Q139. How does Gson's TypeToken work?

new TypeToken<List<String>>(){}.getType() creates an anonymous subclass of

TypeToken<List<String>>, whose generic superclass signature is stored in the class file and read

via reflection.

Q140. Why does an anonymous subclass preserve generic info but a regular instance doesn't?

The subclass declaration extends TypeToken<List<String>> is part of the class file's Signature

attribute; a plain new ArrayList<String>() has no such declaration-level record.

Q141. What does ParameterizedType give you?

A reflection interface exposing the raw type (getRawType()), the actual type arguments

(getActualTypeArguments()), and the owner type.

Q142. How can you create an instance of T in a generic class?

Take a Class<T> (clazz.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance()) or a Supplier<T> (T

t = supplier.get();) as a constructor or method argument.

Q143. What are the risks of T[] arr = (T[]) new Object[n]?

The array's runtime type is Object[], so exposing it as T[] to callers who expect e.g. String[] can

cause ClassCastException. Keep it private and never expose it.

Q144. How do you create a properly typed array using a Class<T>?

T[] arr = (T[]) java.lang.reflect.Array.newInstance(clazz, n); which produces

an array with the correct runtime component type.

Q145. Why does ArrayList store elements in an Object[]?

Because of erasure and generic array restrictions, the implementation uses Object[] internally and

casts elements when returning them.

Q146. What is the difference between toArray(T[]) and toArray(IntFunction<T[]>)?

toArray(T[] a) uses the passed array's runtime type. toArray(IntFunction) (Java 11) lets

you pass String[]::new, which avoids creating a dummy array.

Q147. Can two overloaded generic methods with different bounds coexist?

Yes if their erasures differ, e.g. <T extends Number> void f(T) and <T extends

CharSequence> void f(T) erase to f(Number) and f(CharSequence).

Q148. Can a class implement Comparable<A> and Comparable<B> at once?

No. A class cannot implement the same generic interface with different type arguments, because their

erasures would be identical.

↑ Topic index
Book page 33

Java Generics & Invariance - 200 Interview Questions

Page 14

Q149. Can a generic method declare throws E where E is a type variable?

Yes: <E extends Exception> void run() throws E. It is used for exception-transparent

functional interfaces.

Q150. What is "sneaky throw"?

A trick that uses generics and unchecked casts to throw a checked exception without declaring it:

static <E extends Throwable> void sneaky(Throwable t) throws E { throw (E)

t; }. It exploits erasure and should be avoided in most code.

Q151. Does type erasure affect performance?

There is no runtime generics overhead other than inserted casts, but because primitives can't be type

arguments, boxing/unboxing adds memory and CPU cost.

Q152. What is Project Valhalla in relation to generics?

An OpenJDK effort aimed at value types and specialized generics (e.g. List<int>) to remove boxing

costs. Its delivery status can change, so check the OpenJDK site for current state.

Q153. Where does the compiler insert casts for generics?

At points where erased code returns Object but the source expects a specific type, e.g. String s =

list.get(0); becomes String s = (String) list.get(0);.

Q154. How can you see the effects of erasure in bytecode?

Run javap -c -v ClassName to inspect bytecode, casts, bridge methods, and the Signature

attribute holding generic info.

Q155. What is the Signature attribute in a class file?

Metadata that stores generic declaration information (type parameters, generic supertypes, generic

method signatures) for reflection and the compiler, while executable code uses erased types.

Q156. What does getClass() return for a List<String>?

Class<? extends List> (the erasure of the static type), per the JLS special typing rule for

getClass().

Q157. Is new ArrayList<String>().getClass() == new

ArrayList<Integer>().getClass() true?

Yes. Both are ArrayList.class due to erasure.

Q158. Can erasure cause problems with method overriding in subclasses?

Yes, in rare cases where a subclass method matches a parent's erased signature without being a valid

override, producing a name clash error.

Q159. Why is List<String>[] not reifiable but List<?>[] is?

Arrays require runtime-checkable component types. List<?> is checkable as List, so new

List<?>[10] is legal; List<String> isn't.

Q160. What is the runtime type of T inside a generic method?

There isn't one; T is erased to its bound (or Object), so code like T.class or t instanceof T is

illegal.

Section 5: Generic Methods and Type Inference

↑ Topic index
Book page 34

Java Generics & Invariance - 200 Interview Questions

Page 15

Q161. What is the syntax for a generic method?

public static <T> void print(T item) { ... }. The type parameter section appears

before the return type.

Q162. How can you specify type arguments explicitly when calling a generic method?

Util.<String>emptyList() or this.<String>foo(). You must qualify with a receiver or class

name.

Q163. How does the compiler infer type arguments of a generic method?

From the argument types, and for poly expressions also from the assignment/return target type (target

typing), producing the most specific type that satisfies all constraints.

Q164. Can a non-generic class have generic methods?

Yes. Generic methods are independent of whether the enclosing class is generic.

Q165. What is a generic static factory method?

A static method with its own type parameters that creates an instance, e.g. static <K, V> Map<K,

V> newMap() { return new HashMap<>(); }, to reduce verbosity before the diamond existed.

Q166. When is a generic method better than a wildcard parameter?

When parameters or the return value must be related, e.g. <T> void copy(List<T> a, List<T>

b) or <T> T pick(T a, T b). A wildcard can't express relationships.

Q167. How would you write a generic method that returns the larger of two comparable items?

static <T extends Comparable<? super T>> T max(T a, T b) { return

a.compareTo(b) >= 0 ? a : b; }.

Q168. How do generics interact with varargs?

static <T> List<T> listOf(T... items) creates a generic array implicitly, causing a

heap-pollution warning at call sites; annotate with @SafeVarargs if the body is safe.

Q169. How do lambdas work with generic type inference?

The compiler infers the lambda's parameter and return types from the target functional interface type,

using the inferred type arguments of the surrounding generic method call.

Q170. What is a poly expression?

An expression whose type depends on its target context, such as generic method calls, diamond

instance creation, lambdas, method references, and conditional expressions.

Q171. How does target typing infer List<String> l = Collections.emptyList();?

The assignment target List<String> constrains List<T> so T = String.

Q172. What changed in Java 8 for foo(Collections.emptyList()) when foo takes

List<String>?

Before Java 8 the call failed because inference didn't use the argument position as a target (T inferred

as Object); Java 8 added target typing for method arguments.

Q173. How do method references work with generics?

The compiler infers type arguments from the target functional interface, e.g. Function<String,

Integer> f = Integer::parseInt; and for generic methods like Collections::emptyList it

infers T from context.

↑ Topic index
Book page 35

Java Generics & Invariance - 200 Interview Questions

Page 16

Q174. Can you define your own generic functional interface?

Yes: @FunctionalInterface interface Transformer<A, B> { B apply(A a); }.

Q175. Can a lambda expression be generic?

No. Lambdas cannot declare their own type parameters. A functional interface method may be generic,

but only method references (not lambdas) can implement such a method.

Q176. How can overload resolution become ambiguous with generics?

When two overloads accept different functional interfaces with implicit lambdas of the same shape, or

when erasure/bounds leave several applicable candidates, the compiler reports an ambiguity.

Q177. How does var interact with generics?

var list = new ArrayList<String>(); infers ArrayList<String>. With the diamond, var

list = new ArrayList<>(); infers ArrayList<Object>.

Q178. What does the compiler infer for Arrays.asList(1, "a")?

An intersection type of the common supertypes, such as List<? extends Serializable &

Comparable<...>>, since there is no target type forcing something else.

Q179. What is a generic method's type parameter shadowing?

A method-level type parameter with the same name as a class-level one hides it inside the method,

which is legal but confusing; prefer different names.

Q180. Can you call a generic method with a raw type argument?

Yes, but the call becomes unchecked and the return type is erased, potentially losing type safety.

Q181. What does Collections.<String>emptyList() demonstrate?

An explicit type witness, used when inference fails or the argument position doesn't provide target

typing in older Java versions.

Q182. Does the diamond operator work with anonymous classes?

Since Java 9, yes, provided the inferred type is denotable: Comparator<String> c = new

Comparator<>() { ... };.

Section 6: Advanced Topics, Patterns and Pitfalls

Q183. What is the Type-Safe Heterogeneous Container pattern?

A map keyed by Class<T> whose values are of type T, letting one container hold values of different

types safely (Effective Java Item 33).

Q184. How do you implement a type-safe heterogeneous container?

class Favorites { private Map<Class<?>, Object> m = new HashMap<>(); <T>

void put(Class<T> k, T v) { m.put(k, v); } <T> T get(Class<T> k) { return

k.cast(m.get(k)); } }.

Q185. Why does the heterogeneous container use Class.cast?

It performs a dynamic checked cast that returns T, avoiding unchecked warnings and verifying type

safety at runtime.

↑ Topic index
Book page 36

Java Generics & Invariance - 200 Interview Questions

Page 17

Q186. Why is Class<T> used as a key rather than Class<?>?

Because Class<T> links the key type to the value type at the method signature level:

put(Class<T>, T) ensures the value matches the key.

Q187. How would you implement a generic Visitor pattern?

interface Visitor<R> { R visitA(A a); R visitB(B b); } and interface Node {

<R> R accept(Visitor<R> v); }, letting each visitor choose its own return type.

Q188. How do generics help in the Repository pattern?

interface Repository<T, ID> { Optional<T> findById(ID id); T save(T entity);

} lets one abstraction serve all entity types with compile-time safety.

Q189. How does a framework like Spring resolve generic types for injection?

It uses reflection over generic signatures (fields, constructor params, class hierarchies) through helpers

such as ResolvableType, since runtime instances alone don't carry type arguments.

Q190. What is the classic pitfall when deserializing JSON into a generic type?

mapper.readValue(json, List.class) yields raw List with untyped elements (often maps).

Pass a TypeReference<List<Foo>> to preserve the element type.

Q191. What does Collections.checkedList do?

It returns a dynamically type-checked view that throws ClassCastException on insertion of a

wrongly typed element, catching heap pollution at the source.

Q192. How can mixing raw and parameterized types cause trouble?

Raw type calls bypass checking, so a wrongly typed element can be inserted and detected only later

during retrieval, far from the actual bug.

Q193. Why does using a raw type erase generics for all members of that type?

Under JLS rules, the type of a member of a raw type is the erasure of its type, so even unrelated

generic methods lose their type parameters.

Q194. What happens when a class extends a raw supertype?

The inherited members are erased too, so overriding methods must use erased signatures and callers

lose generic information.

Q195. Can interfaces with generics have default methods?

Yes. Default methods can be generic and use the interface's type parameters, e.g.

Comparator.reversed() or Function.andThen.

Q196. Can enums be generic?

No. enum Foo<T> is illegal. Enums can implement generic interfaces with concrete type arguments.

Q197. Can an inner (non-static) class use the outer class's type parameter?

Yes. Inner class instances are tied to an outer instance, so the outer T is in scope; a static nested class

can't use it.

Q198. What is a generic static nested class?

A static class Node<T> inside another class that declares its own type parameter independent of

the outer one, as in LinkedList.Node.

↑ Topic index
Book page 37

Java Generics & Invariance - 200 Interview Questions

Page 18

Q199. Can anonymous classes be generic?

They can implement or extend a parameterized type (e.g. new Comparator<String>() {...}) but

can't declare their own type parameters.

Q200. How do records work with generics?

Records may be generic: record Pair<A, B>(A first, B second) {}. Type parameters apply

to components and accessors like a normal class.

Q201. How do sealed types combine with generics?

Sealed hierarchies can be generic: sealed interface Result<T> permits Ok, Err {} with

record Ok<T>(T v) implements Result<T> {}, enabling exhaustive pattern matching.

Q202. Can pattern matching with instanceof use parameterized types?

Yes, when the cast is statically safe (checked, not unchecked): if (c instanceof List<String>

l) is allowed when c is a Collection<String>, since no unchecked conversion is needed.

Q203. How do generic record patterns work in switch (Java 21)?

The compiler infers type arguments of the record pattern: switch (r) { case Ok<String>(var

v) -> ...; case Err<String>(var e) -> ...; }, and can infer them in some contexts.

Q204. Why can't you put a value into a Map<String, ?>?

The value type is unknown, so no non-null value is provably safe. Use Map<String, Object> if you

need to put heterogeneous values.

Q205. Is a wildcard return type like List<? extends Number> f() legal?

Yes, but callers receive a read-only-ish view that is awkward to use. Prefer returning a concrete

parameterization.

Q206. What are best practices for designing generic APIs?

Avoid raw types, prefer lists to arrays, use bounded wildcards for flexibility (PECS), don't use wildcards

in return types, minimize unchecked casts, and document type assumptions.

Q207. Which Effective Java items deal with generics?

Item 26 (don't use raw types), 27 (eliminate unchecked warnings), 28 (prefer lists to arrays), 29 (favor

generic types), 30 (favor generic methods), 31 (use bounded wildcards), 32 (combine generics and

varargs judiciously), 33 (typesafe heterogeneous containers).

Q208. What is the result of List<Object> lo = new ArrayList<String>();?

A compile-time error: incompatible types. ArrayList<String> is not a List<Object> because

generics are invariant.

Q209. What happens with List<? super Number> l = new ArrayList<Object>();

l.add(1); Number n = l.get(0);?

l.add(1) compiles (an Integer is a Number), but Number n = l.get(0) fails to compile

because get returns Object (or capture of ? super Number), not Number.

1. Functional Programming Basics

Q1. What is functional programming?

Ans: A programming paradigm that builds programs by composing functions, treating functions as

first-class values, and favoring immutability and side-effect-free computation over mutable state.

Q2. What are the core principles of functional programming?

Ans: Pure functions, immutability, first-class and higher-order functions, function composition,

declarative style, and avoiding shared mutable state.

Q3. What is a pure function?

Ans: A function whose output depends only on its inputs and which causes no side effects (no mutation

of external state, no I/O). Same input always gives same output.

Q4. What is a side effect?

Ans: Any observable change outside a function's return value, such as modifying a field, writing to a file,

printing, or throwing exceptions that affect control flow.

Q5. What is referential transparency?

Ans: An expression is referentially transparent if it can be replaced with its value without changing

program behavior. Pure functions have this property.

Q6. What is a higher-order function?

Ans: A function that takes one or more functions as parameters, returns a function, or both. Examples:

Stream.map(), Comparator.comparing().

Q7. What does "functions as first-class citizens" mean?

Ans: Functions can be assigned to variables, passed as arguments, and returned from methods. In

Java this is achieved through lambdas and functional interfaces.

Q8. Is Java a functional programming language?

Ans: No. Java is primarily object-oriented, but since Java 8 it supports functional features such as

lambdas, method references, streams, and Optional, making it multi-paradigm.

Q9. What is immutability and why does it matter?

Ans: An immutable object cannot change after creation. It is thread-safe by nature, easier to reason

about, and ideal for functional code and parallel processing.

Q10. What is the difference between imperative and declarative programming?

Ans: Imperative code describes HOW to do something step by step (loops, mutation). Declarative code

describes WHAT result is wanted (e.g., stream pipelines).

Q11. What is function composition?

Ans: Combining two or more functions so that the output of one becomes the input of the next. In Java:

Function.andThen() and Function.compose().

Q12. What is currying?

Ans: Transforming a function with multiple arguments into a chain of single-argument functions. In

Java: Function<Integer, Function<Integer, Integer>> add = a -> b -> a + b;

Q13. What is partial application?

Ans: Fixing some arguments of a function to produce a new function with fewer parameters, e.g.,

Function<Integer,Integer> add5 = x -> add.apply(5).apply(x);

Q14. What is lazy evaluation?

Ans: Deferring computation until its result is needed. Java streams evaluate intermediate operations

lazily, only running when a terminal operation is invoked.

Q15. What are the benefits of functional programming in Java?

Ans: Concise code, better readability, easier parallelism, fewer bugs from shared state, improved

testability, and more reusable, composable logic.

2. Lambda Expressions

Q16. What is a lambda expression?

Ans: An anonymous function with optional parameters and a body that can be used wherever a

functional interface is expected. Syntax: (params) -> expression or (params) -> { statements;

}.

Q17. What is the syntax of a lambda expression?

Ans: Three parts: parameter list, arrow token ->, and body. Example: (a, b) -> a + b.

Q18. When can parentheses around lambda parameters be omitted?

Ans: When there is exactly one parameter with an inferred type, e.g., x -> x * 2. Zero or multiple

parameters require parentheses.

Q19. When can braces and the return keyword be omitted?

Ans: When the body is a single expression. The expression's value is returned implicitly.

Multi-statement bodies need braces and an explicit return if a value is returned.

Q20. What is a functional interface?

Ans: An interface with exactly one abstract method (SAM). It can have default, static, and Object-class

methods. Lambdas provide its implementation.

Q21. What is the @FunctionalInterface annotation?

Ans: An optional marker that makes the compiler verify the interface has exactly one abstract method,

producing a compile error otherwise. It documents intent and protects against accidental changes.

Q22. Can a lambda expression exist without a functional interface?

Ans: No. A lambda's type is always inferred from the target functional interface context.

Q23. What is target typing in lambdas?

Ans: The compiler infers the lambda's type from the context where it is used (assignment, method

argument, return statement, cast).

Q24. What are effectively final variables?

Ans: Local variables that are never reassigned after initialization. Lambdas may capture local variables

only if they are final or effectively final.

Q25. Why must captured local variables be effectively final?

Ans: Local variables live on the stack and lambdas may run later or on another thread; capturing a copy

that cannot change avoids inconsistency and thread-safety issues.

Q26. Can a lambda modify instance or static variables?

Ans: Yes. Instance and static fields live on the heap and can be modified, though doing so introduces

side effects and thread-safety concerns.

Q27. What does the "this" keyword refer to inside a lambda?

Ans: The enclosing class instance, not the lambda itself. This differs from anonymous inner classes

where this refers to the anonymous object.

Q28. What are the differences between lambdas and anonymous inner classes?

Ans: Lambdas are shorter, can only implement functional interfaces, do not create a new scope for

this, and are compiled using invokedynamic rather than generating separate class files.

↑ Topic index
Book page 42

Java Functional Programming & Stream API - Interview Q&A | Page 5

Q29. How are lambdas implemented under the hood?

Ans: The compiler turns the body into a private synthetic method and uses invokedynamic with

LambdaMetafactory to create the functional interface instance at runtime.

Q30. Can a lambda throw checked exceptions?

Ans: Only if the functional interface's abstract method declares them. Standard interfaces such as

Function do not, so you must wrap the code in try-catch or use a custom interface.

Q31. How do you handle checked exceptions inside stream lambdas?

Ans: Catch the exception inside the lambda and wrap it in an unchecked exception, or create a wrapper

utility or custom functional interface that rethrows.

Q32. Can lambdas be recursive?

Ans: Not directly because a lambda cannot refer to itself in its initializer. Workarounds include using a

field or class-level variable, or a helper like a Function holder.

Q33. Can a lambda have a variable with the same name as an enclosing local variable?

Ans: No. Lambda parameters and locals cannot shadow local variables of the enclosing scope; this

causes a compile error.

Q34. Are lambdas objects?

Ans: Yes, at runtime a lambda is an instance of the target functional interface, though it is not

necessarily a new object each time (non-capturing lambdas may be cached).

Q35. What is a closure in Java?

Ans: A lambda that captures variables from its enclosing scope. Java closures capture values, not

variables, hence the effectively final rule.

3. Functional Interfaces

Q36. List the main functional interfaces in java.util.function.

Ans: Function, BiFunction, Predicate, BiPredicate, Consumer, BiConsumer, Supplier,

UnaryOperator, BinaryOperator, plus primitive specializations.

Q37. What is the Function interface?

Ans: Function<T,R> has the abstract method R apply(T t). It transforms a value of type T into type

R.

Q38. What is the Predicate interface?

Ans: Predicate<T> has boolean test(T t) and is used for conditions and filtering.

Q39. What is the Consumer interface?

Ans: Consumer<T> has void accept(T t). It performs an operation on a value and returns nothing,

typically with side effects.

Q40. What is the Supplier interface?

Ans: Supplier<T> has T get(). It takes no input and supplies a value, useful for lazy creation.

Q41. What is the BiFunction interface?

Ans: BiFunction<T,U,R> has R apply(T t, U u), taking two arguments and returning a result.

Q42. What is UnaryOperator?

Ans: UnaryOperator<T> extends Function<T,T>; input and output are the same type.

Q43. What is BinaryOperator?

Ans: BinaryOperator<T> extends BiFunction<T,T,T>; two inputs and one output all of the same

type. Also offers static minBy and maxBy.

Q44. What are the default methods of Predicate?

Ans: and(), or(), negate(), and static methods isEqual() and not() (Java 11).

↑ Topic index
Book page 43

Java Functional Programming & Stream API - Interview Q&A | Page 6

Q45. What is the difference between Function.andThen() and Function.compose()?

Ans: f.andThen(g) applies f first then g; f.compose(g) applies g first then f.

Q46. What does Function.identity() do?

Ans: It returns a function that always returns its input argument, commonly used in

Collectors.toMap(Function.identity(), ...).

Q47. What are primitive specializations of functional interfaces and why do they exist?

Ans: Interfaces such as IntPredicate, IntFunction, ToIntFunction, IntSupplier, and

IntBinaryOperator avoid autoboxing overhead for int, long, and double.

Q48. What is the difference between Function and ToIntFunction?

Ans: Function<T,Integer> boxes its result, whereas ToIntFunction<T> returns a primitive int via

applyAsInt, avoiding boxing.

Q49. What is BiConsumer used for?

Ans: It accepts two arguments and returns nothing, e.g., Map.forEach((k, v) -> ...).

Q50. What is BiPredicate?

Ans: BiPredicate<T,U> with boolean test(T t, U u) evaluates a condition on two arguments.

Q51. What is the difference between Runnable, Callable, and Supplier?

Ans: Runnable.run() takes nothing and returns nothing; Callable.call() returns a value and may

throw checked exceptions; Supplier.get() returns a value and throws no checked exceptions.

Q52. How do you create a custom functional interface?

Ans: Declare an interface with a single abstract method, optionally annotated with

@FunctionalInterface, e.g., interface TriFunction<A,B,C,R> { R apply(A a, B b, C c); }.

Q53. Can a functional interface extend another interface?

Ans: Yes, as long as the combined interface still has exactly one abstract method, including inherited

ones.

Q54. Can a functional interface declare methods of Object like equals()?

Ans: Yes. Methods matching public methods of Object do not count toward the single abstract method

limit (e.g., Comparator.equals).

Q55. Is Comparator a functional interface?

Ans: Yes. Its single abstract method is compare(T,T); the many other methods are default or static.

Q56. How do you chain Predicates?

Ans: Use and, or, and negate: Predicate<String> p = isLong.and(startsWithA).negate();

Q57. What are default methods in interfaces and how do they relate to functional

programming?

Ans: Default methods provide concrete behavior inside interfaces, letting APIs like Collection and

Comparator add functional methods without breaking existing implementations.

Q58. Can a functional interface have static methods?

Ans: Yes. Static methods are allowed and do not affect the abstract-method count, e.g.,

Predicate.not().

Q59. What is a Supplier used for in lazy evaluation?

Ans: It delays creation or computation until get() is called, e.g., Optional.orElseGet(Supplier) or

lazy logging.

Q60. How does a lambda decide which functional interface overload to call?

Ans: Through target typing and parameter/return shape. Ambiguity (such as Runnable vs Callable)

can be resolved with a cast or explicit typing.
