1. Thread Basics

Q1. What is a thread in Java?

A thread is the smallest unit of execution inside a process. In Java it is represented by

java.lang.Thread. Threads of one process share the heap but each has its own stack and program

counter.

Q2. What is the difference between a process and a thread?

A process is an independent program with its own memory space; a thread lives inside a process and

shares its memory with sibling threads. Threads are lighter to create and switch between than

processes.

Q3. What is multithreading?

Multithreading is executing multiple threads concurrently within one program to improve

responsiveness, throughput and resource utilization.

Q4. What are the advantages of multithreading?

Better CPU utilization, responsive applications (e.g., UI stays active), true parallelism on multi-core

CPUs, and a natural way to model independent tasks such as handling many client requests.

Q5. What are the disadvantages of multithreading?

Increased complexity, risk of race conditions, deadlocks and visibility bugs, context-switching

overhead, and tests that are hard to reproduce.

Q6. What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism?

Concurrency means managing multiple tasks that make progress in overlapping time periods

(possibly on one core by interleaving). Parallelism means tasks literally run at the same instant on

multiple cores.

Q7. What is the main thread?

The thread the JVM creates to execute the main() method. Other threads are started from it directly

or indirectly.

Q8. What is the difference between a user thread and a daemon thread?

User threads keep the JVM alive until they finish. Daemon threads are background service threads

(e.g., garbage collector); the JVM exits when only daemon threads remain, abruptly stopping them.

Q9. How do you make a thread a daemon thread?

Call thread.setDaemon(true) before start().

Q10. What happens if you call setDaemon() after the thread has started?

An IllegalThreadStateException is thrown, because daemon status can only be changed before

the thread starts.

Q11. What is the default thread priority and its range?

The default is 5 (Thread.NORM_PRIORITY). The range is 1 (MIN_PRIORITY) to 10 (MAX_PRIORITY).

Q12. Does thread priority guarantee execution order?

No. Priority is only a hint to the OS/JVM scheduler. Behavior is platform dependent, so correct

programs must never rely on it.

Q13. What is the thread scheduler?

The part of the JVM/OS that decides which runnable thread gets CPU time and for how long. Its

decisions are not deterministic.

↑ Topic index
Book page 75

Java Threads - 200 Interview Questions & Answers

Page 4

Q14. What is the difference between preemptive scheduling and time slicing?

In preemptive scheduling a higher-priority thread can take the CPU from a lower-priority one. In time

slicing each thread gets a fixed time quantum in turn. Most modern OSes combine both.

Q15. What is context switching?

Saving the state (registers, program counter, stack pointer) of the running thread and loading the

state of another so that the CPU can switch between threads. It has a cost, so too many threads hurts

performance.

Q16. What is the stack size of a thread and how can you change it?

Each platform thread has its own stack (typically 512 KB to 1 MB depending on platform). Change the

default with the JVM option -Xss, or pass a size hint to the Thread constructor. Too many

deep-recursion threads can cause StackOverflowError or OutOfMemoryError.

2. Creating Threads

Q17. In how many ways can you create a thread in Java?

Extend Thread, implement Runnable, implement Callable and submit to an ExecutorService, use

a lambda or method reference for Runnable, use CompletableFuture, or use virtual threads

(Thread.ofVirtual(), Java 21+).

Q18. Which is better: extending Thread or implementing Runnable?

Implementing Runnable is preferred. Java has single inheritance, so extending Thread wastes your

only superclass, and Runnable separates the task from the mechanism that runs it, which allows use

with thread pools.

Q19. What is the difference between Runnable and Callable?

Runnable.run() returns nothing and cannot throw checked exceptions. Callable.call() returns a

value and may throw checked exceptions. Callable is submitted to an executor and its result is

obtained through a Future.

Q20. What is a Future?

A handle to the result of an asynchronous computation. It offers get(), get(timeout), cancel(),

isDone() and isCancelled().

Q21. What happens if you call run() directly instead of start()?

run() executes as a normal method call in the current thread; no new thread is created.

Q22. Why do we call start() and not run()?

start() asks the JVM to allocate a new call stack and native thread, which then invokes run()

concurrently. Calling run() yields no concurrency.

Q23. Can you start a thread twice?

No. A second start() call throws IllegalThreadStateException. A terminated thread cannot be

restarted.

Q24. Can we override the start() method?

Technically yes, but you must call super.start() or no thread will be created. It is rarely a good

idea.

Q25. What is FutureTask?

A class implementing both Runnable and Future. It wraps a Callable so it can be run by a Thread or

executor and its result retrieved later.

↑ Topic index
Book page 76

Java Threads - 200 Interview Questions & Answers

Page 5

Q26. Can a Runnable be written as a lambda expression?

Yes, Runnable is a functional interface: new Thread(() ->

System.out.println("Hi")).start();

Q27. How do you name a thread?

Pass a name to the constructor (new Thread(task, "worker-1")) or call setName(). Good names

make thread dumps and logs easier to read.

Q28. How do you get a reference to the currently executing thread?

Thread.currentThread().

Q29. What is a thread ID?

A unique positive long assigned when the thread is created, returned by threadId() (getId() is

deprecated since Java 19).

Q30. What is a ThreadGroup?

A way to group threads so they can be managed together (e.g., interrupting all). It is largely legacy;

executors and structured concurrency are preferred today.

Q31. What is an UncaughtExceptionHandler?

An interface invoked when a thread terminates due to an uncaught exception. Set per thread with

setUncaughtExceptionHandler() or globally with

Thread.setDefaultUncaughtExceptionHandler().

Q32. What happens if a thread throws an unhandled exception?

That thread terminates and the handler (or default stack trace printing) is invoked. Other threads and

the JVM continue running.

Q33. Can a thread return a value?

Not directly through Runnable. Use Callable with a Future, CompletableFuture, or share state

through thread-safe structures.

Q34. What is the thread-per-request model?

A server design where each incoming request is handled by its own thread. It is simple but platform

threads are expensive, which is why pools and virtual threads exist.

Q35. What are virtual threads?

Lightweight threads introduced as final in Java 21 (Project Loom), managed by the JVM rather than

the OS and mounted on a small pool of carrier threads. They allow millions of blocking tasks cheaply.

Q36. What is the difference between a platform thread and a virtual thread?

A platform thread maps 1:1 to an OS thread and has a large fixed stack. A virtual thread is scheduled

by the JVM, has a small growable stack, and unmounts from its carrier when blocked on I/O.

3. Thread Lifecycle and States

Q37. What are the states of a Java thread?

NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING and TERMINATED (enum Thread.State).

Q38. What is the NEW state?

The thread object has been created but start() has not been called yet.

Q39. Does Java have a RUNNING state?

No. RUNNABLE covers both ready-to-run and actually running; the JVM does not distinguish them.

Q40. What is the BLOCKED state?

The thread is waiting to acquire a monitor lock to enter or re-enter a synchronized block/method.

↑ Topic index
Book page 77

Java Threads - 200 Interview Questions & Answers

Page 6

Q41. What is the WAITING state?

The thread waits indefinitely for another thread's action: Object.wait(), Thread.join() or

LockSupport.park() without a timeout.

Q42. What is the TIMED_WAITING state?

Waiting with a timeout: sleep(ms), wait(ms), join(ms), parkNanos().

Q43. How can you check the current state of a thread?

Call thread.getState().

Q44. Can a terminated thread be restarted?

No. Create a new Thread object instead.

Q45. How does a thread move from WAITING back to RUNNABLE?

Via notify()/notifyAll(), completion of the joined thread, LockSupport.unpark(), or an

interrupt.

Q46. What does isAlive() do?

Returns true if the thread has been started and has not yet terminated.

4. Thread Methods

Q47. What does Thread.sleep() do?

Pauses the current thread for the given time without releasing any locks it holds. It throws

InterruptedException if interrupted.

Q48. Does sleep() release the lock?

No. The thread keeps all monitors it owns while sleeping.

Q49. What is the difference between wait() and sleep()?

wait() belongs to Object, must be called inside a synchronized block, releases the monitor and is

woken by notify. sleep() belongs to Thread, does not need a lock and does not release it.

Q50. What is join() used for?

It makes the calling thread wait until the target thread finishes (or a timeout expires).

Q51. What does Thread.yield() do?

A hint that the current thread is willing to give up the CPU so other runnable threads of the same

priority may run. The scheduler may ignore it.

Q52. What does interrupt() do?

Sets the interrupt flag of the target thread. If the thread is blocked in sleep/wait/join, it wakes up with

InterruptedException and the flag is cleared.

Q53. What is the difference between interrupted() and isInterrupted()?

Thread.interrupted() is static, checks the current thread and clears the flag. isInterrupted() is

an instance method and does not clear it.

Q54. How do you stop a thread safely?

Use cooperative cancellation: the task periodically checks

Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted() (or a volatile flag) and exits cleanly. Request it with

interrupt().

Q55. Why is Thread.stop() deprecated?

It kills the thread abruptly and releases all its locks, possibly leaving shared objects in an inconsistent

state. It is inherently unsafe.

↑ Topic index
Book page 78

Java Threads - 200 Interview Questions & Answers

Page 7

Q56. Why are suspend() and resume() deprecated?

Suspending a thread while it holds locks can easily cause deadlock because the locks are not

released.

Q57. When is InterruptedException thrown?

When a thread is blocked or enters a blocking method (sleep, wait, join, BlockingQueue.take, etc.)

while its interrupt flag is set or becomes set.

Q58. What should you do when you catch InterruptedException?

Either propagate it, or restore the flag with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() and exit.

Swallowing it silently breaks cancellation.

Q59. What is Thread.onSpinWait()?

A hint (Java 9+) that the caller is in a busy-wait loop, letting the CPU optimize (e.g., x86 PAUSE

instruction).

Q60. What does sleep(0) do?

It may let the scheduler run other threads, but behavior is platform dependent and it is not a reliable

yield.

Q61. What does join(timeout) do?

Waits at most the given time for the thread to die, then returns even if the thread is still alive.

5. Synchronization and Thread Safety

Q62. What is a race condition?

A bug where the result depends on the unpredictable timing or interleaving of threads accessing

shared mutable state, e.g., check-then-act or read-modify-write without protection.

Q63. What is a critical section?

A block of code that accesses shared resources and must not be executed by more than one thread

at a time.

Q64. What is synchronization?

A mechanism that controls access to shared resources so that only one thread at a time executes a

critical section, and that also guarantees memory visibility.

Q65. What is the difference between a synchronized method and a synchronized block?

A synchronized method locks this (or the Class object if static) for the whole method. A block locks a

chosen object and only for the needed lines, giving finer-grained, faster code.

Q66. What is the difference between object-level and class-level locking?

Object-level lock protects instance data and is held on this. Class-level lock is held on the Class

object (static synchronized or synchronized(Foo.class)) and protects static data.

Q67. What happens with a static synchronized method?

It acquires the lock of the Class object, shared by all instances.

Q68. What is a monitor or intrinsic lock?

Every Java object has an associated monitor used by synchronized. A thread must own it to execute

synchronized code on that object.

Q69. Is synchronized reentrant?

Yes. A thread that owns a monitor can enter other synchronized blocks on the same object again

without blocking itself.

↑ Topic index
Book page 79

Java Threads - 200 Interview Questions & Answers

Page 8

Q70. Can a constructor be synchronized?

No, the synchronized modifier is not allowed on constructors. You can use a synchronized block

inside the constructor.

Q71. What happens if you synchronize on a null reference?

A NullPointerException is thrown.

Q72. Why should you avoid synchronizing on String literals or boxed Integers?

Interned strings and cached boxed values are shared across the JVM, so unrelated code may

contend on, or deadlock over, the same lock.

Q73. What is thread safety?

A class is thread-safe if it behaves correctly when accessed from multiple threads, without extra

synchronization by callers.

Q74. Why are immutable objects thread safe?

Their state never changes after construction, so there is nothing to race on. Examples: String,

Integer, LocalDate, records with immutable fields.

Q75. What is atomicity?

An operation is atomic if it appears to execute as a single indivisible step, with no intermediate state

visible to other threads.

Q76. Is i++ atomic?

No. It is read, add, write: three steps. Use AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() or synchronization.

Q77. What is the happens-before relationship?

A rule of the Java Memory Model guaranteeing that memory writes by one action are visible to

another. Examples: unlock happens-before subsequent lock, volatile write before volatile read,

start() before actions in the started thread.

Q78. What is the visibility problem?

One thread's write to a variable may not be seen by another thread because of CPU caches or

compiler reordering, unless proper synchronization is used.

Q79. What does the volatile keyword do?

It guarantees that reads see the latest write by any thread and prevents reordering around the

access. It does not provide atomicity for compound actions.

Q80. What is the difference between volatile and synchronized?

Volatile gives only visibility and ordering for a single variable. Synchronized gives mutual exclusion

plus visibility for a whole block.

Q81. Can volatile make count++ thread safe?

No, because the increment is still three separate steps. Use atomics or a lock.

Q82. What is double-checked locking?

A lazy-initialization idiom: check if the instance is null, synchronize, check again, then create. It is

correct in Java 5+ only if the field is volatile.

Q83. Why is volatile required in double-checked locking?

Without it, object construction can be reordered so another thread sees a non-null reference to a

partially constructed object.

Q84. What is the Java Memory Model (JMM)?

The specification that defines how threads interact through memory: what values reads may see and

which reorderings are allowed, via happens-before rules.

↑ Topic index
Book page 80

Java Threads - 200 Interview Questions & Answers

Page 9

Q85. What is instruction reordering?

The compiler, JIT or CPU may reorder independent instructions for performance. Single-thread

semantics are preserved but other threads may observe a different order unless synchronized.

Q86. How do final fields help thread safety?

The JMM guarantees that once a constructor finishes, other threads see correctly initialized final

fields (if this does not escape), without extra synchronization.

Q87. What is a memory barrier (fence)?

A CPU/compiler instruction that prevents certain reorderings of memory operations. The JVM inserts

them for volatile and synchronized.

Q88. What are lock elision and lock coarsening?

JIT optimizations. Elision removes locks on objects that never escape a thread; coarsening merges

adjacent synchronized blocks on the same lock into one.

Q89. What is ThreadLocal?

A class providing variables where each thread has its own independent copy, accessed via get()

and set(). Useful for per-thread context like SimpleDateFormat or request IDs.

Q90. Can ThreadLocal cause memory leaks?

Yes, especially in thread pools: threads live long and their ThreadLocal values stay referenced.

Always call remove() when done.

Q91. What is InheritableThreadLocal?

A ThreadLocal whose value is copied from the parent thread to a child thread at thread creation.

Q92. What is the private lock idiom?

Using a private final Object as the lock instead of this, so outside code cannot interfere by

synchronizing on your object.

Q93. Is synchronized fair?

No. The JVM gives no guarantee about which waiting thread acquires the monitor next, so starvation

is possible.

Q94. What happens to the lock if an exception is thrown inside a synchronized block?

The monitor is released automatically when the block exits, normally or abruptly.

Q95. Can two threads run different synchronized instance methods of the same object at the

same time?

No. Both need the same monitor (this), so one blocks until the other releases it.

Q96. Can one thread run a static synchronized method while another runs a synchronized

instance method?

Yes. They use different locks: the Class object and the instance.

Q97. What is the difference between synchronized collections and concurrent collections?

Synchronized wrappers (Collections.synchronizedList) use one lock for every operation.

Concurrent collections (ConcurrentHashMap, CopyOnWriteArrayList) use finer-grained or lock-free

techniques and scale better.

Q98. Do you need external synchronization when iterating a synchronizedList?

Yes. Iteration is a compound action, so you must hold the list's lock (synchronized(list)) during

the whole iteration.

↑ Topic index
Book page 81

Java Threads - 200 Interview Questions & Answers

Page 10

Q99. Are Vector and Hashtable thread safe?

Yes, their individual methods are synchronized, but they are legacy classes with poor scalability, and

compound operations still need external locking.

Q100. What is the difference between StringBuffer and StringBuilder?

StringBuffer is synchronized (thread safe, slower). StringBuilder is not synchronized and is faster in

single-threaded use.

6. Inter-Thread Communication

Q101. What is inter-thread communication?

A mechanism by which threads coordinate and exchange information, e.g., one thread waits until

another signals that a condition is true. In Java it is done with wait/notify, Conditions, BlockingQueues

and other utilities.

Q102. What are wait(), notify() and notifyAll()?

Methods of Object. wait() releases the monitor and suspends the thread; notify() wakes one

waiting thread; notifyAll() wakes all threads waiting on that object.

Q103. Why are wait(), notify() and notifyAll() defined in the Object class?

Because the lock (monitor) belongs to every object, not to a thread. Threads wait on and signal a

particular object's monitor.

Q104. Why must wait() and notify() be called from a synchronized context?

The calling thread must own the object's monitor; otherwise IllegalMonitorStateException is

thrown. It also prevents lost-wakeup races between checking a condition and waiting.

Q105. What is the difference between notify() and notifyAll()?

notify() wakes one arbitrary waiting thread, which can be wrong if threads wait on different

conditions. notifyAll() wakes all of them and is the safer default.

Q106. Why should wait() always be called in a loop?

To re-check the condition after waking up, because of spurious wakeups and because another thread

may have changed the state before this thread reacquired the lock.

Q107. What is a spurious wakeup?

A thread returning from wait() without having been notified, interrupted or timed out. It is allowed by

the JVM/OS specification.

Q108. What does wait() do with the lock?

It atomically releases the monitor and goes to the wait set. When notified, the thread must reacquire

the monitor before continuing.

Q109. What is the producer-consumer problem?

A classic synchronization problem: producers add items to a bounded buffer and consumers remove

them. Producers must wait when it is full and consumers when it is empty.

Q110. How do you solve producer-consumer using BlockingQueue?

Producers call put() and consumers call take(). The queue blocks automatically when full or empty,

so no manual wait/notify is needed.

Q111. What is a lost wakeup (missed signal)?

A notification sent before the other thread started waiting, so the waiter sleeps forever. Avoided by

guarding with a condition variable checked inside the synchronized region.

↑ Topic index
Book page 82

Java Threads - 200 Interview Questions & Answers

Page 11

Q112. What is the Condition interface?

Created from a Lock with newCondition(). It offers await(), signal() and signalAll(),

equivalent to wait/notify but allowing multiple wait sets per lock.

Q113. What are the advantages of Condition over wait/notify?

Multiple conditions per lock (e.g., notFull and notEmpty), interruptible and timed waits, and

uninterruptible waits, with finer-grained signaling.

Q114. What is an Exchanger?

A synchronization point where two threads swap objects with exchange(). Each blocks until the other

arrives.

Q115. What is a Phaser?

A reusable barrier supporting a dynamic number of parties and multiple phases. It is more flexible

than CyclicBarrier and CountDownLatch.

7. Deadlock, Livelock and Starvation

Q116. What is a deadlock?

Two or more threads each hold a lock and wait forever for a lock held by another, so none can

proceed.

Q117. What are the necessary conditions for a deadlock?

Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Breaking any one prevents

deadlock.

Q118. Can you give an example of a deadlock?

Thread 1 locks A then tries to lock B; Thread 2 locks B then tries to lock A. If each gets its first lock,

both block forever.

Q119. How do you detect a deadlock?

Take a thread dump (jstack <pid>, jcmd <pid> Thread.print, or Ctrl+Break); the JVM reports

deadlocks. Programmatically use ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads().

Q120. How do you prevent deadlocks?

Acquire locks in a consistent global order, hold locks for the shortest time, avoid calling alien methods

while holding locks, use tryLock() with timeouts, and prefer higher-level concurrency utilities.

Q121. What is a livelock?

Threads are not blocked but keep reacting to each other and make no progress, like two people

repeatedly stepping aside in a corridor.

Q122. What is thread starvation?

A thread is perpetually denied access to a resource or CPU time because other threads monopolize

it, e.g., due to unfair locks or low priority.

Q123. What is priority inversion?

A low-priority thread holds a lock needed by a high-priority thread, while medium-priority threads

preempt the low one, effectively delaying the high-priority thread.

Q124. What is the difference between a race condition and a data race?

A data race is unsynchronized concurrent access to the same variable where at least one is a write. A

race condition is a broader logic bug that depends on timing, and can exist even without data races.

↑ Topic index
Book page 83

Java Threads - 200 Interview Questions & Answers

Page 12

Q125. How do you diagnose threading problems in production?

Take several thread dumps, analyze BLOCKED/WAITING threads and lock owners, use profilers

(JFR, VisualVM), check CPU per thread, and enable logging with thread names.

Q126. What is a thread dump?

A snapshot of all threads' states and stack traces at a point in time, used to find deadlocks, hangs and

contention.

Q127. What is thread contention?

Many threads competing for the same lock or resource, causing blocking and reducing throughput.

Q128. What is a spin lock?

A lock where waiting threads loop repeatedly checking the lock instead of sleeping. It is efficient only

for very short critical sections.

Q129. What is busy waiting?

Continuously polling a condition in a loop, wasting CPU cycles. Prefer wait/notify, Conditions or

blocking queues.

Q130. What is a lock-free algorithm?

One that guarantees system-wide progress without using locks, typically through CAS

(compare-and-swap) operations, e.g., ConcurrentLinkedQueue.

8. Locks and Synchronizers

Q131. What is the Lock interface?

In java.util.concurrent.locks, it offers explicit locking with lock(), unlock(), tryLock(),

lockInterruptibly() and newCondition(), more flexible than synchronized.

Q132. What is ReentrantLock?

The standard Lock implementation. It is reentrant: the owning thread may lock it multiple times and

must unlock the same number of times.

Q133. What are the differences between ReentrantLock and synchronized?

ReentrantLock supports tryLock, timed and interruptible acquisition, optional fairness and multiple

Conditions, but needs manual unlock in finally. Synchronized is simpler and releases

automatically.

Q134. What does tryLock() do?

Attempts to acquire the lock without (or with limited) waiting and returns true or false immediately.

Useful to avoid deadlocks.

Q135. What is lockInterruptibly()?

Acquires the lock but allows the waiting thread to be interrupted, throwing InterruptedException.

Q136. What is a fair lock?

new ReentrantLock(true) grants the lock to the longest-waiting thread. It avoids starvation but

lowers throughput.

Q137. What is a ReadWriteLock?

A pair of locks: many readers can hold the read lock concurrently, but the write lock is exclusive.

Good for read-heavy workloads.

Q138. Can a write lock be downgraded to a read lock in ReentrantReadWriteLock?

Yes, acquire the read lock before releasing the write lock. Upgrading from read to write is not

supported and may deadlock.

↑ Topic index
Book page 84

Java Threads - 200 Interview Questions & Answers

Page 13

Q139. What is StampedLock?

A Java 8 lock offering write, read and optimistic read modes using stamps. It is not reentrant and

does not support Conditions.

Q140. What is an optimistic read in StampedLock?

tryOptimisticRead() returns a stamp without locking; after reading data you call validate(stamp)

to check no write occurred, falling back to a real read lock if it did.

Q141. Why should unlock() be placed in a finally block?

To ensure the lock is released even if an exception occurs; otherwise other threads would block

forever.

Q142. What are LockSupport.park() and unpark()?

Low-level primitives to block and unblock threads, used to build locks and synchronizers. A permit

model means unpark before park is not lost.

Q143. What is AbstractQueuedSynchronizer (AQS)?

The framework behind ReentrantLock, Semaphore, CountDownLatch and others, using a volatile int

state and a FIFO queue of waiting threads.

Q144. What is a Semaphore?

A synchronizer holding a number of permits. acquire() takes a permit (blocking if none); release()

returns one. Used to limit concurrent access to a resource.

Q145. What is a CountDownLatch?

A one-time barrier initialized with a count. Threads calling await() block until other threads call

countDown() enough times to reach zero.

Q146. What is a CyclicBarrier?

A barrier where a fixed number of threads wait for each other at a point; after all arrive, it releases

them and can be reused. An optional action runs at each trip.

Q147. What is the difference between CountDownLatch and CyclicBarrier?

Latch is single-use and waiting threads differ from counting threads. Barrier is reusable and all parties

wait for each other.

Q148. What is the difference between a Semaphore and a Mutex?

A mutex allows one owner and is released by the owner. A semaphore allows N permits and any

thread can release, so it has no ownership.

Q149. What is a binary semaphore?

A semaphore with one permit. It acts like a lock but without ownership, so another thread can release

it.

Q150. Can a lock be released by a different thread than the one that acquired it?

Not for ReentrantLock or synchronized (IllegalMonitorStateException). A Semaphore permit,

however, can be released by any thread.

9. Executor Framework and Thread Pools

Q151. What is the Executor framework?

A set of interfaces and classes (Executor, ExecutorService, ScheduledExecutorService,

ThreadPoolExecutor) that decouple task submission from execution policy such as threading and

scheduling.

↑ Topic index
Book page 85

Java Threads - 200 Interview Questions & Answers

Page 14

Q152. What is the difference between Executor, ExecutorService and

ScheduledExecutorService?

Executor only has execute(Runnable). ExecutorService adds lifecycle (shutdown) and

submit/invokeAll. ScheduledExecutorService adds delayed and periodic execution.

Q153. Why use a thread pool?

It reuses threads to avoid creation cost, bounds the number of threads to protect resources, queues

excess work, and provides lifecycle management.

Q154. What is newFixedThreadPool()?

A pool with a fixed number of threads and an unbounded queue of waiting tasks.

Q155. What is newCachedThreadPool()?

A pool that creates threads as needed and reuses idle ones, removing threads idle for 60 seconds. It

can create unbounded numbers of threads.

Q156. What is newSingleThreadExecutor()?

A pool with exactly one worker, executing tasks sequentially in submission order; it replaces the

worker if it dies.

Q157. What is newScheduledThreadPool()?

A pool that can run tasks after a delay or periodically.

Q158. What is newWorkStealingPool()?

Creates a ForkJoinPool with parallelism equal to available processors, where idle threads steal tasks

from busy ones.

Q159. What are the main parameters of ThreadPoolExecutor?

corePoolSize, maximumPoolSize, keepAliveTime, TimeUnit, BlockingQueue, ThreadFactory and

RejectedExecutionHandler.

Q160. How does ThreadPoolExecutor process a submitted task?

If fewer than core threads exist it starts a new thread; else it queues the task; if the queue is full and

threads are below max it starts a new thread; otherwise it rejects the task.

Q161. What are the rejection policies?

AbortPolicy (throws exception, default), CallerRunsPolicy (caller runs the task), DiscardPolicy

(silently drops), DiscardOldestPolicy (drops oldest queued task). You can also implement your

own.

Q162. Which queue types are used with thread pools?

LinkedBlockingQueue (unbounded by default), ArrayBlockingQueue (bounded),

SynchronousQueue (direct handoff, used by cached pool) and PriorityBlockingQueue.

Q163. What is the difference between execute() and submit()?

execute(Runnable) returns nothing and uncaught exceptions go to the thread's handler. submit()

returns a Future and captures exceptions inside it until get().

Q164. What is the difference between shutdown() and shutdownNow()?

shutdown() stops accepting new tasks but finishes queued ones. shutdownNow() attempts to stop

running tasks via interrupt and returns the list of tasks never started.

Q165. What is awaitTermination()?

Blocks until all tasks complete after shutdown, the timeout elapses, or the thread is interrupted.

↑ Topic index
Book page 86

Java Threads - 200 Interview Questions & Answers

Page 15

Q166. What do invokeAll() and invokeAny() do?

invokeAll runs a collection of Callables and returns all Futures when complete. invokeAny returns

the result of one successfully completed task and cancels the others.

Q167. How do you choose the thread pool size?

For CPU-bound work about N cores (+1). For I/O-bound work use N * (1 + wait time / compute time).

Measure and tune under load.

Q168. What is ForkJoinPool?

A pool designed for divide-and-conquer tasks, using work stealing to keep all threads busy. Used by

parallel streams and CompletableFuture default async methods.

Q169. What is work stealing?

Each worker has its own deque of tasks; idle workers steal tasks from the tail of other workers'

deques, balancing the load.

Q170. What is the difference between RecursiveTask and RecursiveAction?

Both are ForkJoinTask subclasses overriding compute(). RecursiveTask returns a result;

RecursiveAction returns nothing.

Q171. What is the common pool and why can parallel streams be risky?

Parallel streams use ForkJoinPool.commonPool() shared by the whole JVM. Blocking or slow tasks

there can starve other users of the pool.

Q172. What is CompletableFuture?

A Future (Java 8+) that supports non-blocking composition: supplyAsync, thenApply, thenCombine,

allOf, anyOf, and manual completion.

Q173. What is the difference between thenApply() and thenCompose()?

thenApply maps the result with a function returning a plain value. thenCompose flattens when the

function itself returns a CompletableFuture (like flatMap).

Q174. How do you handle exceptions in CompletableFuture?

Use exceptionally() to recover, handle() to process both result and error, or whenComplete() for

side effects.

Q175. What happens when you call Future.get()?

It blocks until the result is ready, throws ExecutionException wrapping task failures, or

TimeoutException with the timed variant.

Q176. How do you cancel a Future?

future.cancel(true) tries to cancel and interrupts the running thread if true. The task must

respond to interrupts to stop promptly.

Q177. What is the difference between scheduleAtFixedRate() and scheduleWithFixedDelay()?

FixedRate starts runs at fixed intervals measured from start to start. FixedDelay waits the given delay

after each run finishes.

Q178. What is a ThreadFactory?

An interface to customize thread creation: names, daemon status, priority, exception handlers.

Q179. Why prefer ScheduledExecutorService over Timer?

Timer uses a single thread and one uncaught exception kills it, and it is sensitive to system clock

changes. The executor supports pools and robust error handling.

Java Threads - 200 Interview Questions & Answers

Page 16

Q180. Why do many guidelines discourage the Executors factory methods in production?

Fixed and single pools use unbounded queues (possible OutOfMemoryError) and cached pools

create unbounded threads. A hand-configured ThreadPoolExecutor with bounded queue is safer.

10. Concurrent Collections and Atomics

Q181. How does ConcurrentHashMap work?

It allows concurrent reads and fine-grained updates: Java 8+ uses CAS for empty buckets and

synchronizes only on the head node of a bucket, with treeified bins for heavy collisions.

Q182. What is the difference between ConcurrentHashMap, Hashtable and

Collections.synchronizedMap()?

Hashtable and synchronizedMap lock the entire map for every operation. ConcurrentHashMap locks

per bucket and reads are lock-free, giving far better scalability.

Q183. Does ConcurrentHashMap allow null keys or values?

No. Null would make get() returning null ambiguous in a concurrent setting, so it throws

NullPointerException.

Q184. What is CopyOnWriteArrayList?

A list that creates a new copy of the underlying array on each write. Reads need no locking and

iterators never fail, so it suits read-heavy, rarely modified data.

Q185. What are the BlockingQueue implementations?

ArrayBlockingQueue, LinkedBlockingQueue, PriorityBlockingQueue, DelayQueue,

SynchronousQueue, LinkedTransferQueue and LinkedBlockingDeque.

Q186. What is the difference between ArrayBlockingQueue and LinkedBlockingQueue?

Array-based is always bounded with a single lock. Linked is optionally bounded (default

Integer.MAX_VALUE) and uses separate put and take locks for higher throughput.

Q187. What is ConcurrentLinkedQueue?

An unbounded, non-blocking, thread-safe FIFO queue built on lock-free CAS algorithms.

Q188. What is PriorityBlockingQueue?

An unbounded blocking queue that orders elements by priority (natural order or Comparator); take()

blocks when empty.

Q189. What is SynchronousQueue?

A queue with zero capacity: each insert must wait for a matching remove and vice versa. It is a direct

handoff.

Q190. What is DelayQueue?

An unbounded blocking queue of Delayed elements; an element can be taken only after its delay has

expired.

Q191. What are atomic classes?

Classes in java.util.concurrent.atomic such as AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, AtomicBoolean

and AtomicReference providing lock-free thread-safe operations on single variables.

Q192. What is CAS (Compare-And-Swap)?

A CPU-level atomic instruction that updates a value only if it currently equals an expected value. If it

fails, the thread retries.

↑ Topic index
Book page 88

Java Threads - 200 Interview Questions & Answers

Page 17

Q193. What is the ABA problem?

A value changes from A to B and back to A, so a CAS succeeds even though the state was modified

in between. Solved with versioned references such as AtomicStampedReference.

Q194. What is the difference between AtomicInteger and volatile int?

Volatile ensures visibility only. AtomicInteger also provides atomic compound operations like

incrementAndGet() and compareAndSet().

Q195. What is LongAdder and when is it better than AtomicLong?

LongAdder spreads updates across internal cells to reduce contention, giving higher throughput for

heavy-write counters. Reads (sum()) are slightly slower and not a point-in-time snapshot.

Q196. What is the difference between fail-fast and fail-safe iterators?

Fail-fast iterators (ArrayList, HashMap) throw ConcurrentModificationException if the collection

changes during iteration. Concurrent collections' iterators are weakly consistent or snapshot-based

and do not throw it.

Q197. What is ConcurrentSkipListMap?

A thread-safe sorted map based on skip lists, giving O(log n) operations without locks. It is the

concurrent counterpart of TreeMap.

Q198. When should you use virtual threads instead of platform threads?

For large numbers of blocking, I/O-bound tasks such as web requests. Avoid for CPU-bound work,

and avoid pooling virtual threads. Be careful with long synchronized blocks in older JDKs, which can

pin the carrier thread.

Q199. What are structured concurrency and ScopedValue?

Structured concurrency treats a group of related tasks as one unit of work with a clear lifetime,

simplifying error handling and cancellation. ScopedValue is a lighter alternative to ThreadLocal for

sharing immutable data. Check your JDK version, as these APIs have evolved from preview to final

across releases.

Q200. What are the best practices for writing multithreaded Java code?

Prefer immutability and confinement, use high-level utilities (executors, concurrent collections) over

raw threads, keep lock scope small, acquire locks in a fixed order, always release locks in finally,

handle interrupts properly, name your threads, shut down executors, and test with stress tools.
