1. JVM Architecture Fundamentals

Q1. What is the JVM?

A: The Java Virtual Machine is an abstract computing machine, defined by the JVM Specification, that

loads, verifies and executes Java bytecode. It provides platform independence, automatic memory

management, security and a managed runtime.

Q2. What is the difference between JDK, JRE and JVM?

A: The JVM executes bytecode. The JRE is the JVM plus core class libraries needed to run

applications. The JDK is the JRE plus development tools such as javac, jar, jcmd and jshell.

Since Java 11 a separate JRE is no longer shipped by Oracle; jlink builds custom runtimes.

Q3. What are the major components of the JVM architecture?

A: (1) Class loader subsystem, (2) Runtime data areas (heap, method area/Metaspace, thread

stacks, PC registers, native method stacks), (3) Execution engine (interpreter, JIT compilers, garbage

collector), and (4) Native method interface with native libraries.

Q4. Is the JVM platform independent?

A: No. Java bytecode is platform independent, but each OS/CPU needs its own JVM implementation

that translates bytecode to native instructions.

Q5. What is bytecode?

A: Bytecode is the compact, stack-based instruction set (stored in .class files) produced by javac.

Each opcode is one byte, e.g. iload, invokevirtual, new. You can inspect it with javap -c.

Q6. What is the difference between the JVM specification and a JVM implementation?

A: The specification defines required behavior (class file format, instruction set, runtime areas).

Implementations such as HotSpot, OpenJ9 and GraalVM are free to choose internal designs (GC

algorithms, JIT strategy, object layout) as long as they conform.

Q7. What is HotSpot?

A: HotSpot is the reference JVM implementation in OpenJDK and Oracle JDK. It is named for its

ability to detect "hot" code and compile it adaptively with JIT compilers.

Q8. Is Java compiled or interpreted?

A: Both. Source is compiled to bytecode by javac; at runtime the JVM interprets bytecode initially and

JIT-compiles frequently executed methods to optimized machine code.

Q9. What does "Write Once, Run Anywhere" mean?

A: The same compiled bytecode runs unchanged on any platform that has a conforming JVM,

because the JVM abstracts OS and hardware differences.

Q10. Describe the lifecycle of a JVM instance.

A: It starts when main is launched (bootstrap loader loads the initial class, links and initializes it, then

invokes main). It runs until all non-daemon threads finish, System.exit() is called or a fatal error

occurs. On exit, shutdown hooks run and the JVM terminates.

Q11. What is the difference between daemon and non-daemon threads?

A: The JVM exits when all non-daemon (user) threads complete. Daemon threads (e.g. GC and

compiler threads, or threads marked with setDaemon(true)) do not prevent exit and are abruptly

stopped.

↑ Topic index
Book page 124

Java Memory Model & JVM Architecture - 200 Interview Questions

Page 4

Q12. What are JVM shutdown hooks?

A: Threads registered with Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook() that start when the JVM

begins an orderly shutdown (normal exit, Ctrl+C, SIGTERM). They are not run on kill -9 or a hard

crash, and should be short and thread-safe.

Q13. What is JNI?

A: The Java Native Interface lets Java code call, and be called by, native code written in C/C++. It

uses native methods, System.loadLibrary and the native method stack. Overuse hurts portability

and safety. Project Panama's Foreign Function and Memory API is the modern alternative.

Q14. What is the native method stack?

A: A per-thread area used to execute native (non-Java) methods. In HotSpot it is typically merged

with the Java thread stack.

Q15. What is GraalVM?

A: A high-performance JDK distribution with the Graal JIT compiler (written in Java), support for

polyglot languages and the ability to build ahead-of-time native executables via Native Image, giving

fast startup and low memory use with closed-world limitations.

2. Class Loading and Linking

Q16. What are the phases of class loading?

A: Loading, Linking (verification, preparation, resolution) and Initialization. Classes are loaded lazily,

typically on first active use.

Q17. What happens in the loading phase?

A: A class loader finds the binary representation (.class bytes), parses it and creates a Class object

plus internal metadata in the method area/Metaspace. Superclasses and interfaces are loaded first.

Q18. What does bytecode verification do?

A: It checks that the class file is structurally correct and type-safe (valid stack usage, legal branches,

access rules, no illegal casts) so that malicious or corrupt bytecode cannot compromise the JVM. It

throws VerifyError on failure.

Q19. What happens in the preparation phase?

A: Memory is allocated for static fields and they are set to default values (0, false, null). Explicit

initializers have not run yet, except compile-time constant static final fields that carry a

ConstantValue attribute.

Q20. What is resolution?

A: Replacing symbolic references in the constant pool (class, field, method names) with direct

references. HotSpot usually resolves lazily the first time an instruction uses the reference.

Q21. When does class initialization happen?

A: On first active use: creating an instance with new, calling a static method, reading or writing a

non-constant static field, reflection like Class.forName (with initialize=true), initializing a subclass, or

the class containing main. It runs static initializers and static field initializers in textual order.

Q22. What are the built-in class loaders?

A: Bootstrap loader (native, loads core java.base classes), Platform loader (replaced the Extension

loader in Java 9, loads platform modules) and Application/System loader (loads classpath and

module-path classes).

↑ Topic index
Book page 125

Java Memory Model & JVM Architecture - 200 Interview Questions

Page 5

Q23. Explain the parent delegation model.

A: A class loader first delegates a load request to its parent; only if the parent cannot find the class

does the child try itself. This ensures core classes like java.lang.String come from the bootstrap

loader.

Q24. Why is parent delegation important?

A: It prevents user code from replacing core classes, avoids duplicate loading of the same class and

keeps a consistent, secure type namespace.

Q25. What is the difference between ClassNotFoundException and NoClassDefFoundError?

A: ClassNotFoundException is a checked exception thrown when code explicitly asks to load a class

by name (Class.forName, loadClass) and it is missing. NoClassDefFoundError is an Error thrown

when a class that was present at compile time cannot be found at runtime, or its static initialization

previously failed.

Q26. How and why would you write a custom class loader?

A: Extend ClassLoader and override findClass (preferably not loadClass) to define classes from

bytes. Used for plugin systems, hot reloading, isolation between applications (app servers, OSGi),

encryption or loading from networks/databases.

Q27. What is the difference between Class.forName() and ClassLoader.loadClass()?

A: Class.forName(name) loads and initializes the class (runs static blocks). loadClass(name) only

loads it without initializing, so static blocks run later on first use.

Q28. Can the same class be loaded twice in a JVM?

A: Yes. A class's runtime identity is the pair (fully qualified name, defining class loader). The same

bytes loaded by two loaders yield distinct types, causing ClassCastException when mixed.

Q29. What is a class loader memory leak?

A: A class and its loader cannot be unloaded while something still references them (static fields,

ThreadLocals, threads, JDBC drivers, shutdown hooks). Redeploying web apps repeatedly then

leaks Metaspace and eventually throws OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace.

Q30. How did the Java 9 module system affect class loading?

A: The Extension loader was removed and replaced by the Platform loader; classes are mapped to

named modules, and strong encapsulation restricts reflective access unless packages are opened

(--add-opens).

Q31. What is a static initializer and in what order do initializers run?

A: A static {} block runs once at class initialization. The superclass initializes before the subclass;

static fields and static blocks run in textual order; then, on each new, instance initializers and field

initializers run before the constructor body.

Q32. What is the runtime constant pool?

A: A per-class structure in the method area/Metaspace built from the class file's constant pool. It

holds literals and symbolic references that are resolved at runtime.

Q33. When can classes be unloaded?

A: When the class's defining class loader becomes unreachable and no instances, Class objects or

other references remain. Classes loaded by the bootstrap, platform and application loaders are

effectively never unloaded.

↑ Topic index
Book page 126

Java Memory Model & JVM Architecture - 200 Interview Questions

Page 6

Q34. What is the thread context class loader?

A: A class loader attached to a thread (Thread.getContextClassLoader()) that lets framework

code loaded by a parent loader (e.g. JNDI, JDBC, ServiceLoader) load classes visible only to the

application's child loader.

Q35. Does accessing a compile-time constant trigger class initialization?

A: No. A static final primitive or String initialized with a constant expression is inlined by the

compiler into the caller, so the declaring class is not initialized by reading it.

3. Runtime Data Areas (JVM Memory Structure)

Q36. What are the JVM runtime data areas?

A: Heap, Method Area (Metaspace), JVM Stacks, Program Counter (PC) registers and Native Method

Stacks. Direct memory and the code cache are additional off-heap regions used by HotSpot.

Q37. Which areas are per-thread and which are shared?

A: Per-thread: PC register, JVM stack, native method stack. Shared by all threads: heap and method

area (Metaspace).

Q38. What is the PC register?

A: Each thread has a program counter holding the address of the bytecode instruction currently

executing (undefined while running native methods). It is the only area with no defined

OutOfMemoryError.

Q39. What is the JVM stack?

A: A per-thread LIFO structure of frames. A frame is pushed on each method call and popped when

the method returns or throws.

Q40. What does a stack frame contain?

A: The local variable array, the operand stack, a reference to the runtime constant pool (dynamic

linking) and return address/exception dispatch information.

Q41. What causes StackOverflowError?

A: The thread stack exceeds its allowed size, usually due to infinite or very deep recursion. Fix the

recursion or increase stack size with -Xss.

Q42. What is the heap?

A: The shared area where all objects and arrays are allocated and which the garbage collector

manages. Its size is controlled with -Xms and -Xmx.

Q43. What is the method area?

A: A logical shared area that stores class metadata: field and method data, bytecode, runtime

constant pools and static structure. HotSpot implements it as Metaspace since Java 8.

Q44. What is the difference between PermGen and Metaspace?

A: PermGen was a fixed-size contiguous heap region (-XX:MaxPermSize) that caused frequent

OOMs. Metaspace (Java 8+) lives in native memory, grows dynamically by default and is bounded by

-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize.

↑ Topic index
Book page 127

Java Memory Model & JVM Architecture - 200 Interview Questions

Page 7

Q45. How do you tune Metaspace?

A: Use -XX:MetaspaceSize (initial high-water mark that triggers GC) and -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize

(cap). Investigate leaks from class loaders and generated classes (proxies, bytecode libraries) before

simply raising limits.

Q46. Where are static variables stored?

A: Logically in the method area. In modern HotSpot, static fields of a class live in the heap inside the

java.lang.Class mirror object, while the metadata is in Metaspace.

Q47. Where are string literals stored?

A: In the String Pool (string table), which moved from PermGen to the heap in Java 7, so unused

literals can be garbage collected.

Q48. What does String.intern() do?

A: It returns the canonical pooled instance equal to the string, adding it to the pool if absent. It saves

memory for many duplicates but overuse can slow the string table; compare new String("a") ==

"a" (false) with .intern() == "a" (true).

Q49. How can you tune the string pool?

A: Use -XX:StringTableSize to set the number of buckets (larger reduces collisions), and consider

G1 string deduplication (-XX:+UseStringDeduplication).

Q50. What is the local variable array?

A: A frame-scoped array of slots holding method parameters (including this at index 0) and local

variables. long and double occupy two slots.

Q51. What is the operand stack?

A: A frame-scoped LIFO workspace where bytecode instructions push operands and pop them to

compute results, e.g. iadd pops two ints and pushes their sum.

Q52. What is dynamic linking in a frame?

A: Each frame references the runtime constant pool of its method's class so symbolic references can

be resolved, which also supports late binding for virtual calls.

Q53. What are the common OutOfMemoryError types?

A: Java heap space, GC overhead limit exceeded, Metaspace, unable to create native

thread, Direct buffer memory, Requested array size exceeds VM limit, and Compressed

class space.

Q54. What is the code cache?

A: A native memory region where JIT-compiled machine code is stored. If it fills up, compilation stops

and performance degrades; tune with -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize.

Q55. What is direct (off-heap) memory?

A: Native memory allocated through ByteBuffer.allocateDirect, Unsafe or the FFM API. It avoids

copying for I/O and is not scanned by the GC, but is limited by -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize.

Q56. What are the differences between stack and heap memory?

A: The stack is per-thread, stores frames and primitives/references, is fast, automatically reclaimed

on return and small. The heap is shared, stores objects, is garbage collected and much larger.

↑ Topic index
Book page 128

Java Memory Model & JVM Architecture - 200 Interview Questions

Page 8

Q57. How do you set thread stack size?

A: -Xss512k or -XX:ThreadStackSize, or the stackSize argument of the Thread constructor (a

hint). Larger stacks allow deeper recursion but use more memory per thread.

Q58. Where are local variables and objects stored?

A: Primitives and references are in the frame's local variable array on the stack; the objects they refer

to are on the heap (unless eliminated via escape analysis).

Q59. What is escape analysis?

A: A JIT optimization that proves an object does not escape its method or thread. The compiler can

then do scalar replacement (store fields in registers/stack), lock elision, or avoid heap allocation

entirely.

Q60. How does GC treat Metaspace compared with the heap?

A: Metaspace is not part of the heap and is reclaimed when class loaders become unreachable,

typically during a GC cycle triggered when the Metaspace high-water mark is hit. Heap objects are

reclaimed by generational reachability analysis.

4. Heap Structure and Object Layout

Q61. How is the heap structured in generational collectors?

A: The young generation (Eden plus two Survivor spaces S0/S1) and the old (tenured) generation.

G1 and ZGC use region-based layouts that still model young/old concepts.

Q62. Why use generational collection?

A: The weak generational hypothesis: most objects die young. Collecting a small young area

frequently is cheap, while the old area is collected rarely.

Q63. Describe the lifecycle of an object in the heap.

A: Allocated in Eden; survives a minor GC and is copied to a Survivor space with age incremented;

after reaching the tenuring threshold (or if survivors overflow) it is promoted to the old generation; it is

reclaimed when unreachable.

Q64. What is a TLAB?

A: A Thread-Local Allocation Buffer is a chunk of Eden reserved per thread so that allocation is a fast

pointer bump without locking. Controlled by -XX:+UseTLAB and -XX:TLABSize.

Q65. What is the layout of a Java object in memory?

A: An object header (mark word plus class/klass pointer, plus array length for arrays), then instance

fields (ordered by the JVM), then padding to an 8-byte boundary.

Q66. What is stored in the mark word?

A: Identity hash code, GC age bits, and lock state/pointer information (unlocked, thin lock, inflated

monitor, GC mark). Its encoding varies with lock state.

Q67. What are compressed oops?

A: A technique to store 64-bit object references in 32 bits by using object alignment and a base/shift,

saving

memory

and

cache.

Enabled

by

default

for

heaps

below

roughly

32

GB

(-XX:+UseCompressedOops).

↑ Topic index
Book page 129

Java Memory Model & JVM Architecture - 200 Interview Questions

Page 9

Q68. How large is an empty Object on a 64-bit HotSpot?

A: Typically 16 bytes: 8-byte mark word, 4-byte compressed class pointer and 4 bytes of padding.

Use JOL (Java Object Layout) to verify.

Q69. What is the tenuring threshold?

A: The maximum number of minor GCs an object survives in survivor spaces before promotion

(-XX:MaxTenuringThreshold, default 15). The JVM adapts it dynamically based on survivor

occupancy.

Q70. What is premature promotion?

A: Objects moved to the old generation too early (e.g. survivor space too small, large allocation

bursts) so short-lived data fills old gen and triggers expensive major GCs.

Q71. What are humongous objects in G1?

A: Objects at least half a region size. They are allocated directly in contiguous old-gen "humongous"

regions and can cause fragmentation and extra GC work; tune with -XX:G1HeapRegionSize.

Q72. What is object alignment?

A: Objects are aligned to 8 bytes by default (-XX:ObjectAlignmentInBytes), which enables

compressed oops and cheaper address arithmetic at the cost of padding.

Q73. What are the four reference types?

A: Strong (normal references, never collected while reachable), Soft (cleared before OOM; good for

caches), Weak (cleared at next GC when only weakly reachable) and Phantom (enqueued after

finalization; used for cleanup via ReferenceQueue/Cleaner).

Q74. What is WeakHashMap used for?

A: A map whose keys are held weakly, so entries are removed when keys are no longer strongly

reachable elsewhere. Useful for metadata or canonicalizing caches tied to key lifetime.

Q75. What is finalization and why is it discouraged?

A: finalize() ran before an object was reclaimed. It is unpredictable, slows GC, can resurrect

objects and has been deprecated for removal (Java 18). Use try-with-resources and

java.lang.ref.Cleaner instead.

5. Garbage Collection Fundamentals

Q76. What is garbage collection?

A: Automatic reclamation of heap memory used by objects that are no longer reachable from any live

reference, freeing developers from manual deallocation.

Q77. What are GC roots?

A: Starting points for reachability: local variables and parameters on thread stacks, active threads,

static fields of loaded classes, JNI references and synchronization monitors.

Q78. How does the JVM decide an object is garbage?

A: Through reachability analysis (tracing) from GC roots. Objects not reachable are garbage. Java

does not use reference counting, so cyclic references are collected.

Q79. What are the basic GC algorithms?

A: Mark-sweep (mark live, free dead), mark-compact (also slide live objects together), and copying

(copy live objects to a fresh space). Real collectors combine them.

↑ Topic index
Book page 130

Java Memory Model & JVM Architecture - 200 Interview Questions

Page 10

Q80. How does the copying algorithm work?

A: Live objects are copied from the from-space to an empty to-space and the old space is wiped. It is

fast and fragmentation-free but needs spare space. Used in the young generation.

Q81. What is mark-compact and why use it?

A: After marking, live objects are moved to one end of the region, eliminating fragmentation and

enabling fast bump-pointer allocation, at the cost of moving objects and updating references.

Q82. What is a stop-the-world pause and a safepoint?

A: A pause when all application threads are halted so the JVM can do work (GC, deoptimization,

biased revocation). Threads stop only at safepoints, specific points in code where the thread state is

well defined.

Q83. What is the difference between minor, major, mixed and full GC?

A: Minor collects the young generation. Major collects the old generation. Mixed (G1) collects young

plus some old regions. Full GC collects the entire heap and Metaspace and is usually the most

disruptive.

Q84. What are throughput, latency and footprint in GC tuning?

A: Throughput is the percentage of time spent on application work; latency is pause duration; footprint

is memory used. You generally can optimize two at the expense of the third.

Q85. What are the card table and remembered sets?

A: Structures that record old-to-young (or cross-region) references so that a young collection need

not scan the whole old generation. A card table marks dirty memory chunks; G1 uses per-region

remembered sets.

Q86. What is a write barrier?

A: A small piece of code injected on reference writes that records cross-generation or

concurrent-mark information (updating cards, SATB queues) for the collector.

Q87. What is tri-color marking and SATB?

A: Objects are white (unvisited), gray (visited, children pending) or black (done). Concurrent collectors

must handle mutator changes; Snapshot-At-The-Beginning (G1) records overwritten references so

objects live at the start of marking are not missed.

Q88. What is the difference between parallel and concurrent GC?

A: Parallel uses multiple GC threads while the application is paused. Concurrent runs GC threads

alongside application threads to reduce pauses.

Q89. Can you force garbage collection?

A: System.gc() or Runtime.gc() is only a hint and typically triggers a full GC in HotSpot. It is

considered bad practice outside tests or benchmarks.

Q90. What does -XX:+DisableExplicitGC do?

A: It makes the JVM ignore System.gc() calls. Beware libraries like NIO direct buffers or RMI that

rely on explicit GC; -XX:+ExplicitGCInvokesConcurrent is a gentler option.

Q91. How do you enable GC logging?

A: In Java 9+ use unified logging, e.g. -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags. In Java

8 use -XX:+PrintGCDetails -XX:+PrintGCDateStamps -Xloggc:gc.log.

↑ Topic index
Book page 131

Java Memory Model & JVM Architecture - 200 Interview Questions

Page 11

Q92. Can memory leaks happen in Java? Give examples.

A: Yes: objects that are reachable but no longer needed. Examples are unbounded static collections

or caches, unremoved listeners, ThreadLocals in thread pools, unclosed resources, and class loader

leaks.

Q93. What is OutOfMemoryError: GC overhead limit exceeded?

A: The JVM is spending over about 98 percent of time in GC while recovering less than 2 percent of

the heap. It usually indicates a leak or heap too small. Disabled via -XX:-UseGCOverheadLimit (not

recommended).

Q94. How do you analyze a heap dump?

A: Capture with jmap -dump, jcmd GC.heap_dump or -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError, then

open in Eclipse MAT, VisualVM or JProfiler. Look at the dominator tree, retained sizes and paths to

GC roots.

Q95. What causes long GC pauses?

A: Large live sets, heap too small or too large for the collector, fragmentation leading to full GCs,

humongous allocations, swapping, large reference-processing work, safepoint delays and too few GC

threads.

Q96. What is floating garbage?

A: Objects that become unreachable after the concurrent marking snapshot and therefore survive

until the next cycle.

Q97. What is heap fragmentation?

A: Free memory split into small non-contiguous chunks so a large allocation fails despite enough total

free space. Compacting or copying collectors avoid it.

Q98. What are allocation rate and promotion rate?

A: Allocation rate is how fast the application creates objects (MB/s); promotion rate is how fast data

moves to old gen. High values drive frequent minor GCs and eventual major collections.

Q99. What is GC ergonomics?

A: The JVM automatically selects collector, heap size, generation sizing and thread counts based on

machine resources and goals like -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis and -XX:GCTimeRatio.

Q100. What is generational ZGC?

A: ZGC was extended in Java 21 (JEP 439) with separate young and old generations to improve

throughput and memory efficiency. It became the default ZGC mode in Java 23 and the

non-generational mode was later removed.

6. Garbage Collectors in HotSpot

Q101. What is the Serial collector?

A: A single-threaded, stop-the-world collector for young and old generations (-XX:+UseSerialGC).

Suited to small heaps, single-core or container environments.

Q102. What is the Parallel collector?

A: Also called the throughput collector (-XX:+UseParallelGC). It uses multiple threads for young and

old collections, still stop-the-world, maximizing throughput. It was the default through Java 8.

↑ Topic index
Book page 132

Java Memory Model & JVM Architecture - 200 Interview Questions

Page 12

Q103. What was CMS and what happened to it?

A: Concurrent Mark Sweep was a low-pause old-generation collector that did not compact, leading to

fragmentation and concurrent mode failures. It was deprecated in Java 9 and removed in Java 14.

Q104. What is G1 GC?

A: The Garbage-First collector (-XX:+UseG1GC) divides the heap into equal-sized regions, collects

regions with the most garbage first, does concurrent marking and aims to meet a pause-time goal. It

is the default since Java 9 on server-class machines.

Q105. How does G1 organize the heap?

A: Into 1 to 32 MB regions (power of two) dynamically assigned roles: Eden, Survivor, Old or

Humongous, rather than fixed contiguous generations.

Q106. How does G1 achieve predictable pauses?

A: It estimates the cost of collecting each region and picks a collection set that fits within

-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis (default 200 ms), using remembered sets and incremental evacuation.

Q107. What are mixed collections in G1?

A: After concurrent marking, G1 performs young collections that also evacuate a subset of old regions

with high garbage ratio until reclaimable space falls below a threshold.

Q108. When would you choose G1 over Parallel GC?

A: When you need shorter, more predictable pauses on larger heaps (several GB) and can accept

slightly lower throughput. Parallel suits batch jobs where total throughput matters most.

Q109. What is ZGC?

A: A scalable low-latency collector (-XX:+UseZGC) that does marking, relocation and reference

processing concurrently, targeting pauses typically under a millisecond (a few milliseconds at worst)

regardless of heap size, from MBs up to 16 TB.

Q110. How does ZGC work technically?

A: It uses colored pointers (metadata bits in references, in the original design) and load barriers to

detect stale references and heal them while objects are relocated concurrently. Newer versions use

different pointer encoding but retain load barriers.

Q111. What is Shenandoah?

A: A low-pause, region-based collector (OpenJDK, Red Hat) that performs concurrent evacuation

using Brooks pointers/load reference barriers, with pause times largely independent of heap size.

Q112. What is the Epsilon GC?

A: A no-op collector (-XX:+UseEpsilonGC) that allocates memory but never reclaims it. Used for

performance baselines, short-lived jobs or testing allocation behavior.

Q113. Which GC is the default in each Java version?

A: Java 8: Parallel. Java 9 and later: G1 on server-class machines (2 or more CPUs and 1792 MB or

more memory), otherwise Serial.

Q114. How do you choose the right collector?

A: Small heap or single CPU: Serial. Max throughput/batch: Parallel. Balanced default: G1. Very low

latency or large heaps: ZGC or Shenandoah. Always validate with load tests and GC logs.

↑ Topic index

Page 13

Q115. Which flags enable the main collectors?

A:

-XX:+UseSerialGC,

-XX:+UseParallelGC,

-XX:+UseG1GC,

-XX:+UseZGC,

-XX:+UseShenandoahGC (availability depends on the distribution).

Q116. What does -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis do?

A: It sets a soft pause-time goal for G1 and Parallel. The collector adjusts generation sizes and

collection sets to try to meet it, possibly at the cost of throughput.

Q117. What is InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent?

A: -XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercent (default 45) is the old-gen/heap occupancy at which G1

starts a concurrent marking cycle. Modern G1 also adapts this value automatically.

Q118. What is evacuation failure ("to-space exhausted") in G1?

A: G1 could not find free regions to copy survivors into during a collection, causing a costly fallback

and often a full GC. Increase heap, lower IHOP or reduce allocation pressure.

Q119. What is string deduplication?

A: A G1/ZGC/Shenandoah feature (-XX:+UseStringDeduplication) that makes duplicate String

objects share the same underlying char/byte array to reduce footprint.

Q120. How does the JVM behave in containers?

A: Java 10+ is container-aware, reading cgroup limits for CPU and memory. Use

-XX:MaxRAMPercentage and -XX:InitialRAMPercentage instead of fixed -Xmx, and remember

non-heap memory also counts toward the container limit.

7. Execution Engine and JIT Compilation

Q121. What are the components of the execution engine?

A: The interpreter, JIT compilers (C1 and C2), the garbage collector, and profiling facilities such as

counters used to trigger compilation.

Q122. What does the interpreter do?

A: It executes bytecode instruction by instruction. Startup is fast but execution is slow compared to

compiled code.

Q123. What is the JIT compiler?

A: A just-in-time compiler that translates hot bytecode to optimized native code at runtime using

profile data, often matching or exceeding ahead-of-time compiled code.

Q124. What is the difference between C1 and C2?

A: C1 (client) compiles quickly with modest optimizations. C2 (server) compiles more slowly with

aggressive optimizations (inlining, escape analysis, loop transformations) for peak performance.

Q125. What is tiered compilation?

A: The default mode that starts with interpretation (tier 0), uses C1 with profiling (tiers 1-3), and

moves hot methods to C2 (tier 4), balancing warm-up speed and peak speed.

Q126. How does the JVM identify hot methods?

A: Using invocation counters and back-edge (loop) counters. When thresholds (e.g.

-XX:CompileThreshold in non-tiered mode) are exceeded, the method is queued for compilation.

↑ Topic index
Book page 134

Java Memory Model & JVM Architecture - 200 Interview Questions

Page 14

Q127. What is method inlining?

A: Replacing a call with the callee body, eliminating call overhead and enabling further optimizations.

HotSpot inlines small or hot methods and can speculatively inline virtual calls using type profiles.

Q128. What are common JIT optimizations?

A: Inlining, escape analysis, scalar replacement, lock elision and coarsening, loop unrolling, dead

code elimination, common subexpression elimination, range-check elimination and devirtualization.

Q129. What is deoptimization?

A: Reverting from compiled code to the interpreter when an assumption made by the optimizer (e.g. a

class hierarchy or branch profile) becomes invalid. This may cause temporary slowdowns.

Q130. What is OSR (On-Stack Replacement)?

A: Switching a running method from interpreted to compiled code mid-execution, typically inside a

long-running loop, without waiting for the method to be called again.

Q131. What are lock elision and lock coarsening?

A: Elision removes synchronization on objects proven thread-local by escape analysis. Coarsening

merges adjacent synchronized blocks on the same lock into one larger block.

Q132. What is the "code cache full" problem?

A: The region storing compiled code is exhausted, so the JIT stops compiling new methods and

performance drops. Increase -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize or reduce generated code.

Q133. What is AOT compilation in the Java world?

A: Compiling bytecode to native code before execution. Examples include GraalVM Native Image and

the removed jaotc experiment. It improves startup and footprint but limits dynamic features such as

unrestricted reflection.

Q134. What is JVM warm-up and why does it matter?

A: The period after startup when code is interpreted or lightly compiled. Benchmarks and

latency-sensitive services must account for it; mitigations include CDS, warm-up traffic, and CRaC or

Native Image.

Q135. What are intrinsics?

A: JVM-recognized methods (e.g. Math.sqrt, System.arraycopy, String.indexOf) replaced by

hand-tuned machine code sequences for maximum speed.

Q136. Why is profile-guided optimization an advantage of JIT?

A: The JIT observes real runtime behavior (branch frequencies, receiver types) and optimizes for the

common path, something static compilers can only approximate.

Q137. How can you see which methods are JIT-compiled?

A: Use -XX:+PrintCompilation, or -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintInlining,

and JITWatch for log analysis.

Q138. What are common microbenchmarking pitfalls?

A: Not warming up, dead-code elimination, constant folding, measuring a single run, ignoring GC

noise. Use JMH with Blackhole and proper forks.

Q139. What is Class Data Sharing (CDS)?

A: A feature that maps a pre-parsed archive of class metadata into memory to speed up startup and

enable

sharing

between

JVM

processes.

AppCDS

extends

it

to

application

classes

(-XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit, -XX:SharedArchiveFile).

Q140. What is the difference between JIT and AOT regarding peak performance and startup?

A: JIT has slower startup and warm-up but potentially better peak performance thanks to profiling.

AOT has fast startup and low memory but less adaptive optimization.

8. Java Memory Model (JMM) Core

Q141. What is the Java Memory Model?

A: A part of the Java Language Specification (JSR-133, JLS Chapter 17) defining how threads

interact through memory: which writes become visible to which reads and which reorderings are

permitted. It guarantees behavior across hardware and compilers.

Q142. Why do we need the JMM?

A: Modern CPUs and compilers cache values in registers and cores, and reorder instructions. Without

rules, multithreaded programs would behave differently across platforms. The JMM defines portable

guarantees.

Q143. How does the JMM relate to the JVM runtime data areas?

A: They are different concepts. The runtime data areas describe physical memory organization (heap,

stacks), while the JMM is an abstract model of visibility, ordering and atomicity rules for shared

variables.

Q144. What are working memory and main memory in the JMM?

A: A conceptual model where each thread has a working memory (cache, registers) holding copies of

variables from main memory. Synchronization actions determine when updates are flushed or

refreshed.

Q145. What three properties does concurrency depend on?

A: Atomicity (operations are indivisible), Visibility (one thread's writes are seen by others) and

Ordering (program order appears consistent).

Q146. What is the happens-before relationship?

A: A partial order guaranteeing that if action A happens-before action B, then A's effects (writes) are

visible to B and A is ordered before B. It is the core JMM contract.

Q147. List the main happens-before rules.

A: Program order within a thread; monitor unlock before subsequent lock of the same monitor; volatile

write before subsequent volatile read of the same variable; Thread.start() before any action in the

started thread; all actions in a thread before join() returns; default-value initialization before any

action; object construction end before finalizer start; transitivity.

Q148. What is the program order rule?

A: Each action in a thread happens-before every later action in that same thread, as seen by that

thread. Reordering is allowed only if it is not observable within the thread (as-if-serial).

Q149. What is the monitor lock rule?

A: An unlock of a monitor happens-before every subsequent lock of that same monitor. So everything

done in a synchronized block is visible to the next thread entering a block on the same lock.

↑ Topic index
Book page 136

Java Memory Model & JVM Architecture - 200 Interview Questions

Page 16

Q150. What is the volatile variable rule?

A: A write to a volatile field happens-before every subsequent read of that field. Writes before the

volatile write are also visible after the volatile read.

Q151. What are the Thread start and join rules?

A: A call to start() happens-before any action in the started thread. All actions in a thread

happen-before another thread successfully returns from join() on it.

Q152. Is happens-before transitive?

A: Yes. If A happens-before B and B happens-before C, then A happens-before C. This is how

volatile piggybacking works.

Q153. What is a data race?

A: Two threads access the same variable, at least one is a write, and the accesses are not ordered by

happens-before. Racy programs may observe stale or reordered values.

Q154. What does the volatile keyword guarantee?

A: Visibility of writes across threads and a happens-before ordering on that variable, plus prevention

of certain reorderings around it. It also makes reads and writes of long and double atomic.

Q155. Does volatile make compound operations atomic?

A: No. count++ on a volatile is still read-modify-write and can lose updates. Use AtomicInteger,

synchronized or locks.

Q156. Are reads and writes of long and double atomic?

A: Not necessarily for non-volatile fields: the JLS permits splitting 64-bit access into two 32-bit

operations. Declare them volatile or synchronize. In practice 64-bit JVMs are atomic.

Q157. How is volatile implemented at the hardware level?

A: The JIT inserts memory barriers/fences (e.g. lock-prefixed instructions or mfence on x86, dmb on

ARM) so writes are flushed and reads are not reordered across the volatile access.

Q158. What kinds of reordering can occur?

A: Compiler reordering, CPU out-of-order execution and memory-system reordering (store buffers,

caches). All are allowed if single-thread semantics are preserved.

Q159. What is the as-if-serial semantic?

A: The result of execution within a single thread must be as if instructions executed in program order.

Optimizations may reorder independent operations but not those with data dependencies.

Q160. What does synchronized guarantee?

A: Mutual exclusion plus visibility and ordering: when a thread exits a synchronized block, its writes

are flushed, and a thread entering a block on the same monitor sees them.

Q161. What is the difference between synchronized and volatile?

A: synchronized gives atomicity of a critical section and visibility but can block; volatile gives only

visibility/ordering for a single variable and never blocks. Use volatile for flags and safe publication,

synchronized for compound actions.

Q162. What is double-checked locking and how do you make it correct?

A: Lazy initialization checking null twice, once without lock. It is broken unless the field is volatile

(Java 5+), because otherwise another thread may see a partially constructed object. Alternatives:

initialization-on-demand holder idiom or an enum singleton.

↑ Topic index
Book page 137

Java Memory Model & JVM Architecture - 200 Interview Questions

Page 17

Q163. How can you safely publish an object?

A: Initialize it in a static initializer, store it in a volatile field or AtomicReference, store it in a final field

of a properly constructed object, or guard with a lock/concurrent collection.

Q164. What are the semantics of final fields in the JMM?

A: Once the constructor finishes, other threads see the correct values of final fields (and objects

reachable through them) without synchronization, provided this does not escape during

construction.

Q165. Why are immutable objects thread-safe?

A: Their state cannot change after construction and final field guarantees ensure safe publication of

that state, so no synchronization is needed to share them.

Q166. What are out-of-thin-air values?

A: Reads returning a value that no thread ever wrote. The JMM forbids this even for racy programs,

giving a minimal safety guarantee for references and primitives.

Q167. What does "sequential consistency for data-race-free programs" mean?

A: If a program has no data races, all executions appear as a sequential interleaving of thread

actions, so you can reason without considering reordering.

Q168. What memory effects does ReentrantLock have?

A: lock() and unlock() have the same memory visibility semantics as entering and exiting a

synchronized block: unlock happens-before a subsequent lock of the same lock.

Q169. How do atomic classes work?

A: They use hardware compare-and-swap (CAS) through Unsafe/VarHandle to update values

atomically without locks, and have volatile read/write memory semantics.

Q170. What is the ABA problem?

A: A value changes from A to B and back to A, so a CAS succeeds although state changed in

between. AtomicStampedReference or AtomicMarkableReference addresses it with a version

stamp.

Q171. What are VarHandle access modes?

A: Plain, opaque, acquire/release and volatile, ranging from no ordering to full sequential consistency.

They offer finer-grained memory ordering control than volatile, plus CAS and fences.

Q172. Are interrupts visible across threads?

A: Yes: a call to interrupt() happens-before the interrupted thread detects the interruption (via

InterruptedException or isInterrupted()).

Q173. What is word tearing?

A: Updating one field or array element corrupting adjacent ones on some hardware. Java forbids it:

each field and array element is independent for write operations.

Q174. What is false sharing?

A: Different threads modify independent variables that share the same CPU cache line, causing

cache

invalidation

traffic

and

performance

loss.

Mitigate

via

padding

or

@jdk.internal.vm.annotation.Contended.

↑ Topic index
Book page 138

Java Memory Model & JVM Architecture - 200 Interview Questions

Page 18

Q175. Why can ThreadLocal cause memory leaks?

A: Thread pool threads live long, and entries in a thread's ThreadLocalMap hold strong references to

values. If values (or class loaders through them) are not removed with remove(), they stay reachable.

Q176. What are the thread states in Java?

A: NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING and TERMINATED, from the

Thread.State enum.

Q177. What are the memory semantics of wait() and notify()?

A: They must be called while holding the monitor. wait() releases the lock and re-acquires it on

wake, so writes made before notify under the lock are visible after waking. Always check the

condition in a loop.

Q178. What are deadlock, livelock and starvation?

A: Deadlock: threads wait for each other forever. Livelock: threads keep reacting to each other

without progress. Starvation: a thread never gets resources due to unfair scheduling. Avoid with

consistent lock ordering, timeouts and fair locks.

Q179. What was biased locking?

A: An optimization that favored the first thread to acquire a lock to avoid CAS overhead. It was

deprecated and disabled by default in Java 15 and removed later because its complexity outweighed

benefits.

Q180. Explain lock inflation in HotSpot.

A: Monitors escalate from lightweight (stack-based CAS locking) to heavyweight (OS-level mutex with

wait queues) when contention occurs. Heavyweight locking is more expensive due to parking and

context switching.

Q181. Does happens-before mean "happened earlier in real time"?

A: No. It is a logical visibility guarantee, not a clock ordering. Two actions may occur in time order

without happens-before, in which case visibility is not guaranteed.

Q182. Which JSR defined the modern JMM?

A: JSR-133 (Java 5) fixed flaws in the original model, redefined volatile semantics, final field

semantics and happens-before, and is now part of JLS 17 and the JVM specification.

Q183. Do concurrent collections give visibility guarantees?

A: Yes. Actions in a thread before placing an object into a concurrent collection happen-before

actions after another thread retrieves it (e.g. ConcurrentHashMap, BlockingQueue).

Q184. What happens-before guarantees do Executors and Futures provide?

A: Submitting a task happens-before its execution begins, and task actions happen-before the result

is retrieved through Future.get().

Q185. Does the JMM change with virtual threads?

A: No. Virtual threads (Java 21) follow the same JMM and synchronization semantics. The difference

is scheduling: blocking inside synchronized could pin the carrier thread in older releases, so

ReentrantLock was often recommended.

Q186. Can a thread see stale data without synchronization?

A: Yes. Without happens-before edges, a reader may see an outdated value indefinitely or see writes

out of order.

↑ Topic index
Book page 139

Java Memory Model & JVM Architecture - 200 Interview Questions

Page 19

Q187. Why can a non-volatile boolean flag in a loop hang forever?

A: The JIT may hoist the read out of the loop since no synchronization forces a re-read. Declaring the

flag volatile makes the read fresh each iteration.

Q188. What are memory fences?

A: Instructions preventing reordering across the fence: LoadLoad, LoadStore, StoreLoad and

StoreStore. VarHandle.fullFence(), acquireFence() and releaseFence() expose them in Java.

Q189. What is the difference between effectively final and final?

A: Effectively final means a local variable is never reassigned (usable in lambdas). final is a

declared modifier. Only declared final fields receive the JMM final field freeze semantics.

Q190. What is a memory consistency error?

A: A bug where threads hold inconsistent views of shared data, caused by missing happens-before

relationships, e.g. unsynchronized access to shared mutable state.

9. Tuning, Tools and Troubleshooting

Q191. What do -Xms and -Xmx do?

A: -Xms sets the initial heap size and -Xmx the maximum heap size. Example: -Xms2g -Xmx4g.

Q192. Why is it often recommended to set -Xms equal to -Xmx?

A: It avoids heap resizing pauses and gives predictable memory use, at the cost of reserving memory

upfront. Not always right in memory-constrained containers.

Q193. How do you size generations?

A: -Xmn or -XX:NewSize/MaxNewSize for young gen size, -XX:NewRatio for old/young ratio and

-XX:SurvivorRatio for Eden/Survivor ratio. With G1, prefer pause-goal tuning over manual sizing.

Q194. How would you diagnose high CPU usage in a Java app?

A: Find the process with top, locate hot threads with top -H, convert thread id to hex, then match it in

a jstack thread dump. Alternatively use JFR, async-profiler or jcmd Thread.print.

Q195. Which JDK tools are used for monitoring and troubleshooting?

A: jps, jstat (GC statistics), jmap (heap dumps/histograms), jstack (thread dumps), jcmd

(multi-purpose diagnostic commands), jinfo, JConsole, VisualVM and Java Flight Recorder with

JDK Mission Control.

Q196. How do you read a thread dump?

A: Look at thread states and stack traces; BLOCKED threads show which monitor they wait on and

who owns it ("waiting to lock" vs "locked"). jstack also reports deadlocks. Take several dumps

spaced seconds apart to spot patterns.

Q197. Which flags capture a heap dump on OutOfMemoryError?

A:

-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError

-XX:HeapDumpPath=/path/dump.hprof,

optionally

-XX:OnOutOfMemoryError="..." or -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError.

Q198. What is Java Flight Recorder?

A: A low-overhead event-based profiling and diagnostics framework built into the JVM (free since JDK

11). Start with -XX:StartFlightRecording or jcmd JFR.start, and analyze in JDK Mission

Control.

↑ Topic index
Book page 140

Java Memory Model & JVM Architecture - 200 Interview Questions

Page 20

Q199. How do you diagnose a memory leak step by step?

A: Observe the heap trend after full GCs in GC logs/monitoring, take heap dumps (or class

histograms with jmap -histo) over time, compare them, find dominating objects in MAT, trace GC

root paths and fix the retaining reference.

Q200. What happens end to end when you run java MyApp?

A: The launcher creates the JVM, which initializes runtime areas and GC, the bootstrap loader loads

core classes, the application loader loads MyApp, which is verified, prepared, resolved and initialized.

The main thread invokes main(), bytecode is interpreted and hot code is JIT-compiled, objects are

allocated on the heap and GC reclaims garbage. When non-daemon threads end, shutdown hooks

run and the JVM exits.

1. Clean Code Principles

Q1. What is clean code?

A: Code that is easy to read, understand, change and test: it expresses intent clearly, has minimal

duplication, small focused units and meaningful names. In Robert Martin's words, it reads like

well-written prose.

Q2. Why does clean code matter?

A: Most effort goes into reading and modifying code, not writing it. Clean code lowers bug rates,

speeds up onboarding, reduces maintenance cost and makes safe refactoring possible.

Q3. What is technical debt?

A: The future cost created by shortcuts or poor design chosen now. Like financial debt it accrues

interest (slower changes, more bugs) and should be tracked and repaid deliberately.

Q4. What is the DRY principle?

A: Don't Repeat Yourself: every piece of knowledge should have a single authoritative

representation. Duplicated logic means fixing a bug in several places. Beware of merging code that

only looks similar by accident.

Q5. What is the KISS principle?

A: Keep It Simple, Stupid: prefer the simplest design that works. Complexity multiplies defects and

hinders understanding.

Q6. What is YAGNI?

A: You Aren't Gonna Need It: do not build functionality until it is actually required. Speculative

generality adds code to maintain with no proven value.

Q7. What is the Law of Demeter?

A: A method should talk only to its immediate collaborators (itself, its parameters, its fields, objects it

creates), not reach through chains like a.getB().getC().doIt(). It reduces coupling.

Q8. What is the Boy Scout Rule?

A: Leave the code a little cleaner than you found it. Small continuous improvements prevent code

rot.

Q9. What is separation of concerns?

A: Splitting a program into parts, each handling one distinct responsibility (e.g. web, business logic,

persistence), so changes in one area do not ripple through others.

Q10. Why favor composition over inheritance?

A: Composition is more flexible, avoids fragile base class problems and deep hierarchies, and allows

behavior to be swapped at runtime. Inheritance should model true "is-a" relationships only.

Q11. What is "Tell, Don't Ask"?

A: Tell objects what to do instead of pulling their data and deciding externally. It keeps behavior with

the data and avoids anemic models.

Q12. What is the Principle of Least Astonishment?

A: Code and APIs should behave as most readers would expect. Surprising side effects or

misleading names erode trust and cause bugs.

↑ Topic index
Book page 144

Java Testable and Clean Code - 200 Interview Questions

Page 4

Q13. What are cohesion and coupling?

A: Cohesion measures how strongly the elements of a module belong together; coupling measures

dependency between modules. Aim for high cohesion and low coupling.

Q14. What is Command-Query Separation?

A: A method should either change state (command) or return data (query), not both. This makes

behavior predictable and easier to test.

Q15. What does "fail fast" mean?

A:

Detect

and

report

errors

as

early

as

possible

(validate

arguments,

use

Objects.requireNonNull) rather than letting invalid state propagate and fail obscurely later.

Q16. Why is premature optimization discouraged?

A: Without measurement you often optimize the wrong thing at the cost of readability. Make it correct

and clear first, then profile and optimize hot spots.

Q17. When are comments appropriate?

A: To explain why (intent, trade-offs, workarounds, legal notes) or to document public APIs. Avoid

comments that restate the code or compensate for bad names; refactor instead.

Q18. What is self-documenting code?

A: Code whose names, structure and small functions make its purpose obvious without extra

explanation. Comments then become rare.

Q19. What makes a good code review?

A: Small focused changes, checks for correctness, readability, tests, security and design,

constructive and specific feedback, and automation of style checks so humans focus on substance.

Q20. Which static analysis tools help maintain code quality in Java?

A: Checkstyle (style), PMD and SpotBugs (bug patterns), SonarQube (quality gates, smells,

coverage), Error Prone (compile-time checks) and ArchUnit (architecture rules).

Q21. What is cyclomatic complexity?

A: A metric counting linearly independent paths through a method (roughly decision points plus one).

High values (above about 10) signal hard-to-test, hard-to-read code that should be split.

Q22. Why avoid magic numbers?

A: Unnamed literals hide meaning and are duplicated. Replace them with named constants or

enums such as MAX_RETRIES.

Q23. How does immutability improve code quality?

A: Immutable objects are thread-safe, easy to reason about, safe as map keys and simple to test

since state never changes after construction.

Q24. What are best practices for Java Optional?

A: Use it as a return type for "may be absent" results; do not use it for fields, parameters or

collections; never call get() without checking; prefer map, orElse, orElseThrow.

Q25. How should null be handled cleanly?

A: Avoid returning null (return empty collections, Optional or Null Object), validate inputs early,

annotate with @Nullable/@NonNull, and keep nullable values at the edges.

2. Naming and Readability

↑ Topic index
Book page 145

Java Testable and Clean Code - 200 Interview Questions

Page 5

Q26. What are Java naming conventions?

A: Classes in UpperCamelCase, methods and variables in lowerCamelCase, constants in

UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, packages in lowercase. Interfaces are not prefixed with I.

Q27. What are intention-revealing names?

A: Names that answer why it exists, what it does and how it is used, e.g. elapsedTimeInDays rather

than d. A name that needs a comment is not good enough.

Q28. What does "avoid disinformation" mean in naming?

A: Do not use names that suggest something false, such as calling a Set an accountList or using

names that differ only slightly.

Q29. How should boolean variables and methods be named?

A: As predicates reading naturally in conditions: isActive, hasPermission, canRetry. Avoid

negatives like isNotValid that create double negation.

Q30. How should classes and methods be named?

A: Classes are nouns (InvoiceCalculator); methods are verbs or verb phrases (calculateTotal).

Avoid vague words such as Manager, Helper or Util when a precise name exists.

Q31. How should packages be organized?

A: Prefer package-by-feature (order, payment) for cohesion over package-by-layer (controller,

service, repository) for large codebases; keep package dependencies acyclic.

Q32. Why avoid abbreviations and Hungarian notation?

A: Abbreviations are ambiguous, and type prefixes are redundant in statically typed languages with

IDEs. Use full, pronounceable, searchable names.

Q33. Why does code formatting matter?

A: Consistent formatting improves scanning and reduces diff noise. Use an agreed style (Google

Java Style) enforced by tools such as Spotless or Checkstyle.

Q34. How do guard clauses improve readability?

A: Early returns handle invalid or edge cases first, avoiding deep nesting so the main logic stays at

the lowest indentation.

Q35. When do streams hurt readability?

A: When pipelines are long, have side effects, nested lambdas or complex collectors. Extract steps

into named methods or use a simple loop.

Q36. Lambdas or method references?

A: Use method references when they are clearer (String::trim); use lambdas for short inline logic.

Extract multi-line lambdas into named methods.

Q37. When should you use var?

A: When the type is obvious from the right-hand side (var users = new ArrayList<User>()).

Avoid it when it hides meaning, such as var result = service.process().

Q38. Why prefer enums and constants over strings or ints?

A: They provide type safety, a closed set of values, IDE support and a single place to change.

Enums can carry behavior.

↑ Topic index
Book page 146

Java Testable and Clean Code - 200 Interview Questions

Page 6

Q39. How do you handle long parameter lists?

A: Introduce a parameter object, builder or split the method. More than three or four parameters is

usually a smell.

Q40. Why remove dead code?

A: It confuses readers, rots, and adds maintenance and test burden. Version control keeps history,

so delete rather than comment out.

3. Functions and Methods

Q41. How small should a function be?

A: Small enough to do one thing and be understood at a glance, often under about 20 lines. Size is a

guide; focus and a single level of abstraction matter more.

Q42. What does "do one thing" mean?

A: A function should have one reason to exist; if you can extract another meaningful function from it,

or describe it only with "and", it does more than one thing.

Q43. What are levels of abstraction?

A: Statements in a function should operate at the same conceptual level (e.g. orchestrate steps, not

mix high-level flow with low-level string handling). Read top-down like a story.

Q44. How many arguments should a function have?

A: Ideally zero to two; three is a maximum for most cases. More arguments make usage and testing

harder.

Q45. Why are flag (boolean) arguments a smell?

A: They signal the method does two things and make call sites unreadable (render(true)). Split

into two methods or use an enum.

Q46. What are side effects and why avoid hidden ones?

A: Changes to state outside the function's local scope (fields, I/O, globals). Hidden side effects

surprise callers and make tests brittle; make them explicit in the name or isolate them.

Q47. What are pure functions?

A: Functions whose output depends only on inputs and which have no side effects. They are

deterministic, thread-safe and trivial to test.

Q48. Return error codes or throw exceptions?

A: Throw exceptions for exceptional conditions; error codes force callers to check and clutter logic.

Use return types like Optional or Result for expected absence or failure.

Q49. Checked or unchecked exceptions?

A: Checked for recoverable conditions callers can reasonably handle; unchecked for programming

errors. Many modern frameworks favor unchecked exceptions to avoid signature pollution.

Q50. Why not return null from methods?

A: Callers must remember null checks, and omissions cause NullPointerException. Return an empty

collection, Optional or Null Object.

↑ Topic index
Book page 147

Java Testable and Clean Code - 200 Interview Questions

Page 7

Q51. When should you create custom exceptions?

A: When callers need to distinguish or handle a failure specifically or add domain meaning

(InsufficientFundsException). Include context and preserve the cause.

Q52. Why is swallowing exceptions bad?

A: Empty catch blocks hide failures and make debugging impossible. Handle, rethrow with context or

at least log with the stack trace.

Q53. What is try-with-resources?

A: A construct that automatically closes AutoCloseable resources, even on exceptions, avoiding

leaks and verbose finally blocks, and recording suppressed exceptions.

Q54. What is the Extract Method refactoring?

A: Moving a code fragment into a new, well-named method to remove duplication, shorten long

methods and clarify intent.

Q55. How do you replace large switch statements?

A: With polymorphism (Strategy, State, or an enum with abstract methods) or a map of handlers, so

adding a case does not require editing existing code (Open/Closed).

4. Classes, SOLID and Object Design

Q56. What is SOLID?

A: Five design principles: Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface

Segregation and Dependency Inversion. They promote maintainable, flexible object-oriented design.

Q57. What is the Single Responsibility Principle?

A: A class should have one reason to change, i.e. serve one actor or concern. This keeps classes

cohesive and small.

Q58. Give an example of an SRP violation.

A: A UserService that validates input, hashes passwords, saves to the database, sends emails and

formats reports. Split into focused collaborators.

Q59. What is the Open/Closed Principle?

A: Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification: add new behavior by

adding code (new implementations) instead of editing tested code.

Q60. How do you apply OCP in Java?

A: With abstractions (interfaces, abstract classes), Strategy or Decorator patterns, and dependency

injection, so new variants plug in without changing existing classes.

Q61. What is the Liskov Substitution Principle?

A: Subtypes must be usable wherever their base type is expected without breaking correctness:

same contracts, no stronger preconditions, no weaker postconditions.

Q62. What is a classic LSP violation?

A: A Square extending Rectangle where setting width also changes height breaks callers'

assumptions. Also subclasses that throw UnsupportedOperationException for inherited methods.

↑ Topic index
Book page 148

Java Testable and Clean Code - 200 Interview Questions

Page 8

Q63. What is the Interface Segregation Principle?

A: Clients should not depend on methods they do not use. Prefer several small, role-specific

interfaces over one fat interface.

Q64. What is the Dependency Inversion Principle?

A: High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both depend on abstractions, and

abstractions should not depend on details.

Q65. What is the difference between DIP, IoC and DI?

A: DIP is a design principle. Inversion of Control is the broader idea of a framework controlling flow

and object creation. Dependency Injection is a technique implementing IoC by supplying

dependencies from outside.

Q66. How do you judge class size and cohesion?

A: Classes should be small with fields used by most methods (high cohesion). If subsets of methods

use disjoint subsets of fields, split the class.

Q67. What is encapsulation?

A: Hiding internal state and exposing behavior through a minimal public API so invariants are

protected and internals can change freely.

Q68. Abstract class or interface?

A: Interfaces define capabilities/contracts and allow multiple implementation; abstract classes share

state and partial implementation in a single inheritance chain. Prefer interfaces, add abstract base

classes only for shared code.

Q69. What are concerns with default methods?

A: They can blur contracts, introduce diamond conflicts and encourage putting logic in interfaces.

Use them mainly for backward-compatible API evolution.

Q70. What is an anemic domain model?

A: Domain objects that hold only data with getters/setters while logic lives in services. It spreads

rules and weakens encapsulation; move behavior into the entities.

Q71. What is a rich domain model?

A: Entities and value objects that encapsulate both state and business rules, enforcing invariants

themselves (Domain-Driven Design).

Q72. Objects versus data structures?

A: Objects hide data and expose behavior; data structures expose data and have little behavior.

Mixing the two (hybrids) yields the worst of both. DTOs are intentional data structures at boundaries.

Q73. What are Java records and when to use them?

A: Records (Java 16) are concise immutable data carriers with generated constructor, accessors,

equals, hashCode and toString. Ideal for DTOs and value objects; they allow compact constructors

for validation.

Q74. What are sealed classes?

A: Classes or interfaces that restrict which types may extend them (sealed ... permits).

Combined with pattern matching they enable exhaustive, closed hierarchies.

↑ Topic index
Book page 149

Java Testable and Clean Code - 200 Interview Questions

Page 9

Q75. What is a value object?

A: An immutable object defined by its attributes, not identity (Money, Email). Equal values are

interchangeable, which removes primitive obsession and centralizes validation.

Q76. What is the equals/hashCode contract?

A: Equal objects must have equal hash codes; equals must be reflexive, symmetric, transitive,

consistent and false for null. Override both together using the same fields.

Q77. When is the Builder pattern useful?

A: For objects with many optional parameters or needing validated, immutable construction,

replacing telescoping constructors with readable fluent code.

Q78. What are the downsides of static and utility classes?

A: They cannot be overridden or injected, hide dependencies, encourage procedural code and are

hard to mock. Fine for stateless pure helpers.

Q79. Why is the Singleton often a problem?

A: It is global mutable state, hides dependencies, complicates testing and parallel tests. Let a DI

container manage single instances instead.

Q80. What is a God class?

A: A class that knows and does too much, with many responsibilities and dependencies. Break it up

by extracting cohesive classes.

Q81. What is feature envy?

A: A method more interested in another class's data than its own. Move it to the class whose data it

uses.

Q82. What are common pitfalls of inheritance?

A: Tight coupling to base class internals (fragile base class), broken encapsulation, deep hierarchies

and LSP violations. Prefer composition and mark classes final by default.

Q83. What are fluent interfaces?

A: APIs designed for method chaining that read like a sentence (builders, streams). Useful for

readability, but avoid when chaining hides side effects.

Q84. What is package-by-feature?

A: Grouping classes by business capability so related code lives together, enabling package-private

visibility and modularization, versus technical layering.

Q85. What are Hexagonal (Ports and Adapters) and Clean Architecture?

A: Architectures placing domain logic at the center, independent of frameworks, databases and UI,

which interact through ports (interfaces) and adapters. Dependencies point inward, which makes the

core easy to test.

5. Code Smells, Refactoring and Patterns

Q86. What is a code smell?

A: A surface symptom in code suggesting a deeper design problem, such as long methods or

duplicated code. It is not a bug but a hint to refactor.

↑ Topic index
Book page 150

Java Testable and Clean Code - 200 Interview Questions

Page 10

Q87. Name common code smells.

A: Long method, large class, long parameter list, duplicated code, feature envy, primitive obsession,

shotgun surgery, divergent change, data clumps, switch statements, dead code and comments used

as deodorant.

Q88. What is refactoring?

A: Restructuring existing code without changing its external behavior to improve design, readability

and maintainability, supported by automated tests.

Q89. When should you refactor?

A: Continuously: before adding a feature to ease it (preparatory refactoring), while fixing bugs, during

review, and when you spot smells. Avoid large unplanned rewrites.

Q90. How do you refactor safely?

A: Have tests (or write characterization tests) first, make small steps, run tests after each, use IDE

automated refactorings and commit frequently.

Q91. What is the Strategy pattern?

A: Encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind an interface so behavior can be chosen at

runtime, replacing conditionals.

Q92. What is the Factory pattern?

A: Centralizes object creation behind a method or class so callers depend on abstractions, not

concrete constructors.

Q93. What is the Decorator pattern?

A: Wraps an object to add behavior dynamically while keeping the same interface (e.g.

BufferedInputStream), an alternative to subclassing.

Q94. What is the Observer pattern?

A: Subjects notify registered observers of state changes without tight coupling. Seen in event

listeners and Spring application events.

Q95. What is the Template Method pattern?

A: A base class defines an algorithm skeleton, deferring specific steps to subclasses. Consider

Strategy for composition-based alternatives.

Q96. What is the Adapter pattern?

A: Converts one interface into another expected by clients, useful for wrapping third-party or legacy

APIs.

Q97. What is the Facade pattern?

A: Provides a simplified interface to a complex subsystem, reducing coupling to its internals.

Q98. What is the Null Object pattern?

A: A harmless default implementation that does nothing, replacing null checks (e.g. NoOpLogger).

Q99. What is the Specification pattern?

A: Business rules encapsulated as composable predicate objects (and, or, not), making complex

criteria reusable and testable.

↑ Topic index
Book page 151

Java Testable and Clean Code - 200 Interview Questions

Page 11

Q100. What is "Replace Conditional with Polymorphism"?

A: Moving each branch of a type-based conditional into a subclass or strategy so behavior is

selected by the object's type.

Q101. What is primitive obsession?

A: Using primitives or strings for domain concepts (money, phone numbers). Replace with value

objects carrying validation and behavior.

Q102. What is shotgun surgery?

A: One change forces many small edits across many classes, indicating a responsibility scattered.

Consolidate it into one class or module.

Q103. What is divergent change?

A: One class changes for many unrelated reasons, a symptom of SRP violation. Split it by reason for

change.

Q104. How do you remove duplicated code?

A: Extract method, extract class, pull up method, use template method or strategy, or parametrize.

Verify the duplicates truly represent the same concept.

Q105. What is Introduce Parameter Object?

A: Replace groups of parameters that travel together with a single object, shortening signatures and

giving the concept a home.

Q106. What is Replace Magic Number with Constant?

A: Substituting unexplained literals with named constants or enums to document meaning and

centralize changes.

Q107. How do you approach legacy code without tests?

A: Add characterization tests to pin current behavior, find seams to break dependencies, make small

safe changes, and refactor under test (Michael Feathers' approach).

Q108. What is the Strangler Fig pattern?

A: Incrementally replacing a legacy system by routing functionality piece by piece to new

implementations until the old one can be retired.

Q109. What are common Java anti-patterns?

A: God object, singleton overuse, constant interface, exception swallowing, returning null collections,

premature optimization, spaghetti code, copy-paste programming and the Service Locator.

Q110. What is over-engineering?

A: Adding abstraction, patterns or flexibility beyond current needs. It increases complexity; apply

patterns only to solve real problems (YAGNI).

6. Unit Testing Fundamentals

Q111. What is a unit test?

A: An automated test that verifies a small unit of behavior (typically a class or method) in isolation,

fast and deterministic.

↑ Topic index
Book page 152

Java Testable and Clean Code - 200 Interview Questions

Page 12

Q112. Unit vs integration vs end-to-end tests?

A: Unit tests check isolated logic; integration tests verify collaboration with real components (DB,

HTTP); end-to-end tests exercise the complete system through the UI or API. Cost and runtime

increase in that order.

Q113. What is the test pyramid?

A: A guideline recommending many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests and very few end-to-end

tests, for quick feedback and low maintenance.

Q114. What does FIRST stand for?

A: Fast, Independent, Repeatable, Self-validating, Timely. Properties of good unit tests.

Q115. What is the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern?

A: Structure a test into setup (Arrange), executing the behavior (Act) and verifying results (Assert). It

maps to Given-When-Then.

Q116. Should a test have one assertion?

A: Aim for one logical concept per test, which may require several assertions on the same outcome

(use assertAll). Avoid testing unrelated behaviors together.

Q117. How should tests be named?

A: Describe behavior and context, e.g. shouldRejectOrder_whenStockIsInsufficient or use

@DisplayName, so failures read as a specification.

Q118. What makes code testable?

A: Small cohesive units, dependency injection, no hidden static or global state, deterministic

behavior, separation of logic from I/O, and clear inputs and outputs.

Q119. What are test doubles?

A: Stand-ins for real collaborators: dummy, stub, spy, mock and fake (Gerard Meszaros' taxonomy).

Q120. What is the difference between a mock and a stub?

A: A stub returns canned answers to calls (state verification); a mock also records interactions so

tests verify behavior (e.g. that a method was called).

Q121. What is a spy?

A: A wrapper around a real object that records calls and allows partial stubbing.

Q122. What is a fake?

A: A working lightweight implementation, such as an in-memory repository, used in place of a heavy

real dependency.

Q123. Is 100% code coverage a good goal?

A: No. Coverage shows executed code, not verified behavior. Pursue meaningful assertions and

risk-based coverage; a high but sensible target (around 70 to 90 percent) with quality tests is more

useful.

Q124. Line vs branch coverage?

A: Line coverage measures executed lines; branch coverage measures each decision outcome

(true/false). Branch coverage is stricter and more informative.

Q125. What is mutation testing?

A: Tools like PIT introduce small code changes (mutants) and check that tests fail. Surviving mutants

reveal weak tests.

Q126. What causes flaky tests?

A: Shared state, timing and sleeps, concurrency, random or time-dependent data, external services,

and ordering dependencies. Fix by isolating, using fake clocks and awaiting conditions.

Q127. Why must tests be isolated?

A: Tests that depend on order or shared state fail unpredictably. Each test should set up and clean

up its own state.

Q128. Should you test private methods?

A: Generally no; test them through the public API. If a private method is complex enough to need

direct tests, extract it into its own class.

Q129. How do you test that an exception is thrown?

A:

With

assertThrows

in

JUnit

5

(also

verifying

message

or

cause),

or

AssertJ

assertThatThrownBy.

Q130. What are parameterized tests?

A: One test method run with multiple data sets (@ParameterizedTest with @ValueSource,

@CsvSource, @MethodSource), reducing duplication and covering edge cases.

Q131. What are Test Data Builders and Object Mother?

A: Patterns for creating test objects: Builders offer fluent customization with sensible defaults; Object

Mother provides prebuilt named fixtures. Builders scale better.

Q132. How do you test time-dependent code?

A: Inject a java.time.Clock (or a time provider) and use a fixed clock in tests instead of calling

LocalDateTime.now() directly.

Q133. How do you test code involving randomness?

A: Inject the random source or seed it, so tests are deterministic; or test properties rather than exact

values.

Q134. How do you test code that calls static methods?

A: Wrap them behind an injectable interface, or as a last resort use Mockito mockStatic in a limited

scope.

Q135. How do you add tests to legacy code?

A: Find seams, write characterization tests around existing behavior, then refactor and extend with

new unit tests.

Q136. What are common test smells?

A: Excessive mocking, logic in tests, fragile tests tied to implementation, slow tests, obscure test

(unclear setup), eager tests, and shared mutable fixtures.

Q137. How do you test void methods?

A: Verify side effects: state changes, interactions with mocks (verify), captured arguments, thrown

exceptions or output.

Q138. What is a test fixture and where should setup live?

A: Known state needed for tests. Use @BeforeEach for shared minimal setup, but prefer helper

methods or builders so each test remains readable.

Q139. What is property-based testing?

A: Instead of fixed examples, define properties that must hold for any input and let a framework

(jqwik) generate many random cases and shrink failures.

Q140. What are golden master (approval) tests?

A: Tests capturing the current output of a system and comparing future outputs against it. Useful for

legacy code with complex outputs (ApprovalTests library).

7. JUnit 5 and Mockito

Q141. What is the architecture of JUnit 5?

A: JUnit Platform (launching tests), JUnit Jupiter (new programming and extension model) and JUnit

Vintage (runs JUnit 3/4 tests).

Q142. What are key differences between JUnit 4 and JUnit 5?

A: Package org.junit.jupiter, @BeforeEach instead of @Before, @Disabled instead of @Ignore,

extensions instead of runners and rules, lambdas support, @Nested, parameterized tests built in, and

Java 8+ requirement.

Q143. What are the lifecycle annotations in JUnit 5?

A: @BeforeAll, @BeforeEach, @AfterEach, @AfterAll. By default a new test instance is created per

method; @TestInstance(PER_CLASS) changes that.

Q144. What is @Nested used for?

A: Grouping tests in inner classes that model contexts (e.g. "when empty"), sharing setup

hierarchically for readable structure.

Q145. What does @DisplayName do?

A: Provides a custom human-readable test name for reports, supporting spaces and emojis.

Q146. What is assertAll?

A: Groups multiple assertions so all are executed and failures reported together instead of stopping

at the first.

Q147. How does assertThrows work?

A: It executes a lambda, expects a specific exception type and returns the exception for further

assertions.

Q148. What sources can parameterized tests use?

A:

@ValueSource,

@EnumSource,

@CsvSource,

@CsvFileSource,

@MethodSource

and

@ArgumentsSource.

Q149. What is @TempDir?

A: An annotation injecting a temporary directory that JUnit creates and deletes automatically,

simplifying file I/O tests.
