Q150. What are JUnit 5 extensions?

A: A mechanism (@ExtendWith) to hook into the lifecycle: parameter resolution, conditional

execution, callbacks. Examples are MockitoExtension and SpringExtension.

Q151. How do you disable or filter tests?

A: @Disabled, conditions (@EnabledOnOs, @EnabledIfEnvironmentVariable) and @Tag with build

tool filters.

Q152. Why use AssertJ instead of plain assertions?

A:

Fluent,

readable,

type-aware

assertions

with

rich

failure

messages

(assertThat(list).hasSize(2).contains("a")), richer than Hamcrest or JUnit asserts.

Q153. What are the basics of Mockito?

A:

mock(Class)

creates

a

mock,

when(...).thenReturn(...)

stubs

behavior,

and

verify(mock).method() checks interactions.

Q154. What do @Mock, @InjectMocks and MockitoExtension do?

A: @Mock creates mocks, @InjectMocks creates the tested object injecting mocks (constructor,

setter or field), and @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) initializes them and enforces strict

stubs.

Q155. What is ArgumentCaptor?

A: A Mockito utility capturing arguments passed to mocks so you can assert on their properties.

Q156. What is the rule for argument matchers?

A: If one argument uses a matcher (any(), eq()), all arguments in that call must use matchers.

Q157. When do you use doReturn().when() instead of when().thenReturn()?

A: For spies and void or throwing stubs, since when(spy.method()) actually invokes the real

method.

Q158. What is the difference between mock and spy in Mockito?

A: A mock replaces all behavior with defaults; a spy wraps a real object, calling real methods unless

stubbed.

Q159. How do you verify call counts and order?

A: verify(mock, times(2)), never(), atLeastOnce(), and InOrder for sequence verification.

Q160. What are strict stubs and UnnecessaryStubbingException?

A: With the Mockito extension, unused stubs fail the test, keeping tests clean. Remove the stub or

use lenient() if justified.

Q161. How do you mock static methods in Mockito?

A: Use Mockito.mockStatic(Class) inside try-with-resources (needs the inline mock maker,

default since Mockito 5). Prefer redesign to avoid it.

Q162. Can Mockito mock final classes?

A: Yes, with the inline mock maker (default since Mockito 5). Older versions required configuration.

Q163. What is a Mockito Answer?

A: A callback computing return values dynamically from invocation arguments via thenAnswer.

Q164. What is BDDMockito?

A: A syntax using given(...).willReturn(...) and then(mock).should() aligning stubbing and

verification with Given-When-Then.

Q165. What is over-mocking?

A: Mocking everything, including simple collaborators and value objects, making tests mirror

implementation and break on refactoring. Mock only boundaries and slow or nondeterministic

dependencies.

8. TDD, BDD and Test Strategy

Q166. What is TDD?

A: Test-Driven Development: write a failing test (Red), write minimal code to pass (Green), then

refactor (Refactor), repeating in short cycles.

Q167. What are the benefits of TDD?

A: Better design (testable, decoupled), fast feedback, a regression safety net, living documentation

and less over-engineering.

Q168. What are the drawbacks of TDD?

A: Learning curve, initial slowdown, poorly suited to exploratory or UI-heavy work, and risk of brittle

tests if tied to implementation details.

Q169. What are the London and Chicago schools of TDD?

A: Chicago (classicist) uses real objects and state verification; London (mockist) isolates units with

mocks and verifies interactions, driving design outside-in.

Q170. What is BDD?

A: Behavior-Driven Development extends TDD by describing behavior in business-readable

language (Given/When/Then), improving collaboration between developers, QA and stakeholders.

Q171. What is Cucumber?

A: A BDD tool executing Gherkin feature files by mapping steps to Java step definitions.

Q172. What is ATDD?

A: Acceptance Test-Driven Development: acceptance criteria are written as automated tests before

implementation to define done.

Q173. What is contract testing?

A: Verifying that a consumer and provider of an API agree on a contract (Pact, Spring Cloud

Contract), catching integration breakages without full end-to-end environments.

Q174. What is Testcontainers?

A: A library that runs real dependencies (databases, Kafka, Redis) in disposable Docker containers

for realistic, reproducible integration tests.

Q175. How do you test database code?

A: Use real databases via Testcontainers when possible, roll back or clean between tests, and avoid

in-memory DBs when SQL dialect differences matter.

Q176. How do you test REST APIs?

A: MockMvc or WebTestClient for slice tests, RestAssured for HTTP-level tests, and WireMock to

stub external services.

Q177. How do tests fit in CI/CD?

A: Fast unit tests on every commit, integration tests in pipeline stages, quality gates for coverage

and static analysis, and fail the build on broken tests.

Q178. What is ArchUnit?

A: A library for writing unit tests that enforce architecture rules (layering, package dependencies,

naming) in Java code.

Q179. How do you test concurrent code?

A: Make logic deterministic by isolating shared state, use latches, Awaitility for async assertions,

stress tests and tools like jcstress; avoid Thread.sleep.

Q180. How should a bug fix be handled in a test-driven way?

A: First write a failing test reproducing the bug, then fix it, so the regression stays covered.

9. Designing for Testability

Q181. How does dependency injection improve testability?

A: Dependencies are passed in, so tests can substitute fakes or mocks without changing code or

using reflection.

Q182. Constructor injection or field injection?

A: Prefer constructor injection: dependencies are explicit and final, objects are valid after

construction and tests can instantiate them without a container.

Q183. What is a seam?

A: A place where behavior can be altered without editing the code at that place (interface,

overridable method, injected dependency), enabling isolation in tests.

Q184. How do you isolate third-party libraries?

A: Wrap them behind your own interface (port) with an adapter, so domain code depends on the

abstraction and tests substitute a fake.

Q185. Why abstract the clock?

A: LocalDate.now() makes tests time-dependent. Injecting Clock gives deterministic tests for

expiries, schedules and timestamps.

Q186. Why avoid static mutable state?

A: It leaks between tests, prevents parallel execution and creates hidden dependencies. Prefer

injected instances.

Q187. Why is new inside business logic a testability issue?

A: Hard-wired creation of collaborators cannot be replaced in tests. Inject factories or the

dependencies themselves.

Q188. How does the Law of Demeter help tests?

A: Fewer chained calls means fewer mocks to wire and less coupling to object graphs.

Page 18

Q189. How does immutability help testing?

A: No hidden state changes: objects can be shared across tests and assertions are simpler.

Q190. What is "functional core, imperative shell"?

A: Keep business logic as pure functions (core) and push I/O and side effects to a thin outer layer

(shell). The core is tested with simple unit tests.

Q191. How do you test asynchronous code?

A: Return CompletableFuture/Future and join with timeouts, use Awaitility for polling assertions,

inject executors (run synchronously in tests) and avoid sleeps.

Q192. How do you test logging?

A: Usually do not; if logs are a requirement, use a test appender (Logback ListAppender) or a

logging abstraction. Test behavior, not log text.

Q193. How do you test file I/O?

A: Use JUnit @TempDir, abstract file access behind an interface or use in-memory file systems like

Jimfs.

Q194. What are pitfalls of using H2 in tests?

A: SQL dialect and feature differences from the production database can hide bugs. Prefer

Testcontainers with the real engine.

Q195. Does designing for testability mean interfaces everywhere?

A: No. Interfaces with a single implementation add noise. Introduce them at real boundaries or when

substitution is needed; mock concrete classes otherwise.

Q196. How does dependency inversion benefit testing?

A: Core logic depends on abstractions, so it can be tested without databases or frameworks using

in-memory fakes.

Q197. Why should constructors avoid doing real work?

A: Work such as I/O or complex logic in constructors makes objects hard to instantiate in tests and

hides failures. Keep constructors to assignment and validation.

Q198. How do you test code that uses singletons?

A: Inject the singleton through an interface or let a DI container manage scope; avoid

getInstance() calls inside logic.

Q199. What is test-induced design damage?

A: Distorting production design (excess interfaces, exposing internals, indirection) solely to ease

testing. Balance by testing behavior at proper boundaries and refining the design.

Q200. What is a checklist for clean, testable code?

A: Small focused units, meaningful names, explicit dependencies via constructors, no hidden

globals, pure logic separated from side effects, fast deterministic tests, high-value coverage,

automated style and quality checks, and continuous refactoring.
